title: TPM22: Oakland, NWSA back Long Beach data project
content: The Port of Long Beach’s Supply Chain Information Highway was announced in late December, with a goal of harmonizing supply chain data for importers and exporters across US container gateways. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A Port of Long Beach initiative to provide a platform for container freight data for US shippers has been boosted by support from two other West Coast gateways. The Port of Oakland and the Northwest Seaport Alliance of Seattle and Tacoma (NWSA) this week signaled their support for Long Beach’s “Supply Chain Information Highway” project, a free service meant to aggregate container information for shippers and other stakeholders to integrate into their own systems. Long Beach announced plans for the platform Dec. 22, but the initiative was formally unveiled at JOC’s TPM22 Conference earlier this week. Port of Long Beach Deputy Executive Director Noel Hacegaba told conference attendees the system is designed to complement existing for-profit data and visibility platforms, not replace them. In its first phase, which is now operational, the project will focus on container visibility events, Hacegaba said, with the platform eventually expanding to incorporate other data elements. To account for the reality that most US importers and exporters move goods through more than one port, Hacegaba said Long Beach understood the need for its platform to provide information at other US gateways. Support from Oakland and the NWSA is a step in that direction. “Creating a shared digital platform will provide decision makers timely, comprehensive and quality data,” Port of Oakland Maritime Director Bryan Brandes said in a statement Thursday. “Having this cargo visibility tool can help speed the supply chain and set a digital foundation for improving goods movement.” Long Beach and its technology vendor, St. Louis-based UNCOMN, have for the past few months been gathering and normalizing container event data for a pilot involving a marine terminal operator, a group of transportation providers, and several shippers. “Members of the testing phase group were invited to transmit data, query data, and validate the results,” the port said in the statement. Complicating Long Beach’s initiative is the fact the neighboring Port of Los Angeles has its own container data platform, called the “Port Optimizer,” which provides a range of free and paid tools for shippers and other port users. While the Port Optimizer captures truck turn time data for all terminals in Los Angeles and Long Beach, other data elements, including average dwell times, are only available for Los Angeles terminals. The ports likely see the provision of data as a key competitive differentiator. Still, splitting the terminals into two data camps crimps the ability of users to assess container availability across the entire gateway. Additionally, there have been calls by major US shippers for the Federal Maritime Commission to take the lead in establishing a national port data portal. That was echoed by Peter Creeden, managing director of maritime consultant MPC International, during a session Feb. 24 at the TPMTech Conference in Long Beach. Creeden argued that ports need to invest in their digital infrastructure as they have in physical infrastructure, with the establishment of a common data portal across gateways an effective way to serve port users. Meanwhile, shippers and forwarders have said cargo data accuracy is a bigger hurdle than access. Robert Khachatryan, CEO of Los Angeles-based forwarder Freight Right, told TPM22 that it’s a challenge to manage divergent information about container status, “and that the data is always changing.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. Complicating Long Beach’s initiative is the fact the neighboring Port of Los Angeles has its own container data platform, called the “Port Optimizer,” which provides a range of free and paid tools for shippers and other port users. While the Port Optimizer captures truck turn time data for all terminals in Los Angeles and Long Beach, other data elements, including average dwell times, are only available for Los Angeles terminals. Creeden argued that ports need to invest in their digital infrastructure as they have in physical infrastructure, with the establishment of a common data portal across gateways an effective way to serve port users. Meanwhile, shippers and forwarders have said cargo data accuracy is a bigger hurdle than access. title: Forto follows Flexport into multi-billion dollar valuation
content: Forto has raised $540 million over the past 16 months, turning demand during the pandemic into a trove of cash to build its product and expand its physical footprint. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. German forwarder Forto has landed a $250 million block of funding to achieve a $2.1 billion valuation as high-profile venture capital groups continue to build the coffers of digitally native intermediaries. It comes weeks after Forto’s US competitor Flexport announced its own $935 million funding round. Forto’s latest round, led by Austin-based venture firm Disruptive, comes less than nine months after a $240 million investment led by SoftBank, which also invested in the new round. In all, Forto has raised $600 million — $540 million of which has come in the last 16 months. It said Monday it will use the new funding to improve its customer interface and expand to new offices in Europe. The company, founded in 2016, has focused on serving European shippers via its Asian offices in Shanghai, Ningbo, Shenzhen, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Ho Chi Minh City, and European offices in Rotterdam, Madrid, Copenhagen, and Aarhus, Denmark, as well as its headquarters in Berlin. Forto said it plans to expand to customers in Poland, Belgium, Sweden, and southern Europe in 2022. Investment into the digital forwarding model has accelerated throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, with a range of Forto’s European competitors, including Zencargo and Beacon, landing early-stage funding rounds. The model is also garnering investment in Latin America, where Nowports has been backed by venture firm Tiger Global, and Oceania, where Explorate landed a funding round in January. The fact that funding has not been concentrated into Flexport alone — even if the San Francisco-based forwarder has snapped up the lion’s share of overall VC investment — signals that investors see the forwarding market as a fragmented one. Shipping analyst Lars Jensen told TPM22 last week in Long Beach he expects to see “tens of thousands” of small or mid-sized forwarders go out of business over the course of the next decade as competition heightens among VC-backed intermediaries, well-capitalized incumbents, e-commerce marketplaces, and container lines wanting to vertically integrate. Ulrik Sanders, a managing director and senior partner at consulting firm BCG, similarly noted the intense competition to lure shippers with digital solutions during a keynote address at TPM22. He added that even marine terminal operating groups, such as DP World and PSA International, are offering logistics services that were once only the province of forwarders. “It used to be clear what everyone was doing,” but the lines have blurred, Sanders said. Industry skeptics argue that digital forwarders are not doing much fundamentally different than incumbents and are merely using huge cash infusions to subsidize rates or rebrand products that forwarders have long before offered. But it’s clear that digitally native forwarders are growing; Flexport said its revenue increased from $1.3 billion in 2020 to $3.3 billion in 2021. Forto has not publicly released financial figures. Aside from expanding its physical footprint, Forto said the funding will also be used to refine its interface with customers, where it focuses on how to “simplify interactions, remove process friction, and increase visibility around the supply chain.” Forto called its round “pre-emptive,” alluding to a financing term where a company raises funding prior to when they might ordinarily need it. “We recognize that this is an exceptionally challenging period for many of our customers,” Forto CEO Michael Wax said in the statement. “As our business remains well-funded from our previous round in 2021, this new round will simply allow us to accelerate the execution of our existing strategy, particularly on our geographic expansion.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Size matters: How Walmart and Target dominated amid disruption, inflation
content: For many companies, an unexpected bill for $400 million would be a crucible, if not the beginning of a tailspin. For Walmart, the world’s largest company by revenue, it was a mere speed bump. That figure, $400 million, was what the company spent on supply chain costs above management’s original estimates for the fourth quarter, which ultimately yielded some $3.6 billion in net income. For the two legacy, mass merchant giants Walmart and Target, a year of unprecedented supply chain turmoil raised costs and posed some challenges, to be sure. But their scale and vast financial resources allowed them to absorb that disruption. Their ability to stock shelves kept Walmart and Target’s sales growth strong — piled on top of surging growth for both in 2020 — and in large part helped them to offset the cost of getting goods into the country and to their stores. Both retailers have a fine line to walk on prices, which have spiked throughout the economy with supply chain costs. To differing degrees, Walmart and Target rely on value in their brand promises to customers, to make themselves destinations. Yet they are operating in inflationary times, watching their costs increase while competitors hike prices and struggle to stock their own shelves. RBC Capital Markets analyst Steven Shemesh said in a February note, ahead of Walmart’s earnings release, that the retail giant was among the “better positioned to offset cost pressures.” That is thanks in no small measure to financial firepower. “At this point, it’s well understood that Walmart has elected to eat a portion of supplier price increases to maintain low prices for customers,” Shemesh said. At the same time, Walmart and Target also pulled back on discounts and sales for customers, which also helped their bottom lines. The industry’s struggles to stock inventory during Q4 and the year more generally makes it that much easier for everyone to pullback on sales promotions. Source: Walmart investor materials. Note: Except for inventory, all metrics are for Walmart U.S. Walmart’s gross margin rate increased by a “healthy” 54 basis points in Q4, which “reflecting primarily price management resulting from cost increases in mix,” Walmart Chief Financial Officer Brett Biggs said in the company’s February earnings call. In other words, the company did nudge prices up to manage its own rising costs. In a world of rising prices, though, a price decrease is a competitive edge. Walmart has the deep pockets and the leverage with suppliers to do it, even now. Walmart CEO Doug McMillon during the call that it was “working closely with our suppliers to manage inflation, finding a few places where we can roll back prices.” For Walmart, price itself may not be as important as “price gaps” — the difference in price tags between Walmart and its competitors. “We’re constantly monitoring our share, our price gaps to competitors,” said John Furner, chief of Walmart U.S. “And we’ll continue to do that as we move forward. And then what we’re seeing right now is not only gaps that we’re proud of that are valuable for our customers, but we’re also seeing the opportunity to increase some of our rollbacks in stores.” And while Walmart tried to navigate its pricing to maintain customer perceptions of value, its inventory position provided another differentiator. “Going into the period, some competitors appeared tight on inventory, but Walmart seemed well positioned,” said analysts with MKM Partners in a note just ahead of the retailer’s earnings announcement, noting that the retailer’s inventory was up 11% year over year at the beginning of the period. As with pricing, Walmart’s deep pockets helped in that regard. It famously chartered ships and made many other moves, large and small, to ensure it was stocked for the holidays. Walmart has also taken a few pages out of rival Amazon’s playbook and developed a few side hustles that during the quarter and year helped buffer its bottom line from supply and freight cost increases. Its advertising business passed $2 billion dollars, while its membership revenue (which includes both its Sam’s Club and Walmart+ memberships) added billions more. The retailer has also launched third-party fulfillment and delivery services it is selling to other retailers and brands. Walmart Fulfillment Services grew 500% last year, as the company looks to increase the seller base to its online marketplace while also giving those sellers a reason to spend advertising dollars with the company. Target, meanwhile, was similarly able to use its size and scale to grow its sales and navigate supply chain turmoil. The retailer’s comps rose 8.9% in the fourth quarter and 12.7% during the fiscal year. And even as it absorbed higher freight, supply chain and merchandise costs, its operating profit and margin rate grew thanks to higher sales. Target did not say how much it spent on supply chain cost increases. But the company also navigated them through its merchandising mix, presumably emphasizing higher-margin goods, and held back on customer promotions. While the retailer is willing to slow its discounts, it appears hesitant to raise prices more than needed. “We have many levers to combat costs, and price is the one we pull last, not first,” Michael Fiddelke, Target chief financial officer, said during a recorded investor call last week. “As a result, product costs within our assortment have risen faster than retail’s in recent quarters, reflecting this intentional approach and deliberate pacing. We expect this trend to continue, particularly in the first half of this year as we maintain our focus on affordability for our guests.” The retailer, along with Walmart, touted its agile supply chain as the holiday period began and talk of a crisis started filling the news. Target hired en masse for its supply chain, moved containers to bypass the congested Long Beach and Los Angeles ports, increased night pickups, and ran its supply chain operations 24-hours a day, among other efforts. “We have the global scale to keep the product people want and need moving through our pipeline,” CEO Brian Cornell said during the investor call. Yet, Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData, pointed to product shortages, including in holiday decorations and sundries, during the period. Saunders told Retail Dive in an email that some Target shops were ”looking spartan towards the end of the period.” But Saunders also noted that “with supply chain issues affecting all retailers, Target was not alone in this and given the elevated demand it faced, we believe it handled the holiday period very well.”

title: Bolloré-backed startup Ovrsea expands digital forwarding options to US
content: Ovrsea, founded in 2017, tied up a strategic partnership with Bolloré in early 2021, with the French logistics group taking an ownership stake in the Paris-based startup. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. French forwarder Ovrsea is expanding its footprint to North America as it seeks to explore growth in the US and Canada due in part to a strategic partnership it signed with the Bolloré Group a year ago. Ovrsea is among a cohort of international intermediaries to emerge over the past decade that are nominally dubbed digital forwarders, but the Paris-based company has largely operated under the radar since its founding in 2017. Unlike some of its peers, most notably Flexport and Forto, Ovrsea has taken on limited venture capital to date, instead building through word of mouth and its alliance with Bolloré. That partnership, in which Bolloré purchased a majority share of Ovrsea, has driven growth in the startup’s customer base to the extent that the company was compelled to open a physical office in New York, CEO Arthur Barillas told JOC.com in an interview. Ovrsea has more than 100 US-based customers already, he added, primarily in the chemicals, e-commerce, cosmetics, and high-tech verticals. Its customers typically move in the range of 200 to 1,000 TEU annually. “When they are above that, they have their own way in the market, and smaller than that, they are less in need of our capabilities in terms of integration,” Barillas said. Being part of the Bolloré Group has accelerated the company’s growth, he said. “One thing we can bring is that we’re part of a group that gives network effects [through access to Bolloré customers, freight capacity, and warehousing assets], which increases our firepower to customers in the US and Asia,” Barillas said. “So we have the firepower and scale effects of a large group with the technology and service of a startup.” Calling it a “best of both worlds” scenario, Barillas echoed an oft-repeated mantra about the hurdles that independent digitally oriented forwarders face. “You either have to work with startups without scale, or legacy players with huge network effects, but without the same service- and product-centricity,” he said. Barillas said Ovrsea didn’t have a dedicated salesperson until February. Until then, it relied on early export customers in France to spread the word among their import counterparts in the US. That cycle drew not just the US importers onto Ovrsea’s platform, but also other partners of those importers. The Bolloré partnership has been key. A year ago, Ovrsea was in the process of raising a venture capital round of funding — it has previously raised about $2.1 million — until Bolloré stepped in to take an ownership stake while allowing Ovrsea to operate independently. Terms of the investment were not disclosed. “We didn’t expect a corporate to have the same vision of startup, but they did,” Barillas said. “We have not felt pressure to change our mindset, and they bring us a network of physical assets, their offices, their procurement power, and their know-how and expertise.” Ovrsea, meanwhile, gives Bolloré a chip to play in the fast-evolving digital side of global logistics. Aside from defined digital forwarders such as Flexport and Forto, liner carriers such as Maersk and Zim have established digital forwarding entities, while terminal operators such as DP World are even in the game. Agility recently spun out its Shipa Freight entity as an independent forwarder after selling a piece of its business to DSV in April 2021. German forwarder Leshaco spun out its in-house technology platform as a separate entity, called Logward, in 2018. That’s aside from forwarding marketplaces, such as Freightos and FreightMango, and the wide range of software providers that aim to enable existing forwarders. “The market is moving in the direction of digitally native,” Barillas said. “They are majority investors, so there’s financial upside for them the more we grow. But we also help them grow their digital assets and address their own digital transformation.” Barillas said Ovrsea tries to differentiate from its digitally native peers by investing heavily in engineering. He said 20 percent of employees are dedicated to product and technology. “That’s fundamentally different than traditional forwarders,” he said. Ovrsea is specifically focused on helping shippers manage freight quotes, tender requests, and measurement of their carbon footprints. Another point of emphasis is empowering shippers to make in-the-moment decisions around their contract allocations with container lines, and when to switch to a freight-all-kinds (FAK) spot rate. “It’s built around day-to-day requirements for shippers,” he said. “We’re trying to make it easier for shippers to do what they do. So we send quotes within two hours. We integrate our platform with their [enterprise resourcing planning system] and [transportation management system]. A lot of what we invest, the customer doesn’t see, because it’s automating the everyday operations.” Barillas also said it’s fair to judge the efficiency of digitally native forwarders by their revenue per full-time employee as a measure of how much technology is doing the work of executing shipments and managing disruptions versus relying on people to do that work. Barillas also addressed a long-discussed quandary around digital forwarding: whether digitally enabled intermediaries are better placed to innovate than pure software vendors selling their product to existing forwarders. He argued that software developed internally enables a forwarder to ensure it is actually being used by its operations teams. “There are so many evolutions in terms of operations,” he said. “Just being able to push the new version of software within the company to catch up with new issues from carriers or customs. If we weren’t doing this internally, it’s difficult to envision how you get people to change their habits.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. He argued that software developed internally enables a forwarder to ensure it is actually being used by its operations teams. “There are so many evolutions in terms of operations,” he said. “Just being able to push the new version of software within the company to catch up with new issues from carriers or customs. If we weren’t doing this internally, it’s difficult to envision how you get people to change their habits.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. title: 'Price-wage spiral' boosting inflation: Moody's
content: CFOs confront the harshest inflationary pressures in decades, with bottlenecks in the supply of semiconductors, metals and other inputs pushing up the producer price index 9.7% last year. They passed on to consumers some of the higher cost — the CPI in 2021 rose 7%. Labor markets are also extremely tight, with workforce participation falling below pre-pandemic levels. Companies competing for workers pushed up average hourly earnings 5.7% in January compared with 12 months before, the Labor Department said Friday. Worker shortages have prompted predictions that U.S. companies will try to improve employee hiring and retention by pushing up wages as much as 5.2% this year. The finding by Moody’s that wage gains lag increases in prices suggests that employment cost pressures will ease if supply disruptions wane, slowing the rise in producer prices. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell has forecast that supply chain bottlenecks will start to clear and inflation will begin to cool during the summer. At the same time, recent wage gains will likely lure more workers back into the job market and ease pressure for further increases in compensation. “The good news about the acceleration in nominal wage growth is that labor supply constraints should be less binding,” Moody’s said. Wage increases have spurred growth in the labor force since the mid-1960s, Moody’s said. “Workers normally have a sense of the minimum they will accept — also known as a reservation wage — to take a job.” “With nominal wage growth accelerating, it should pull more people into the labor force this year,” Moody’s said. “An end to the pandemic would also be key” to coaxing workers off the sidelines. As of the end of December, wage gains had not caught up to price increases, suggesting the two are not reinforcing one another in a pattern of rising inflation, Deloitte said in a recent report. “Although wages have accelerated sharply, they continue to rise more slowly than prices, thereby rendering workers with less purchasing power,” Deloitte said. “This means that we have not yet seen the start of a wage-price spiral that would contribute to prolonged inflation.”

title: Loadsure snags funding round to drive real-time freight insurance
content: Loadsure’s aim is to make the freight insurance quoting and settlement process more real-time and efficient. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Loadsure, a London-based company that has predominantly provided insurance technology to the US freight industry, has landed an $11 million funding round from a group of investors, including maritime logistics provider Crowley. The funding will be used to grow Loadsure’s reach, including to international modes and the intermediaries that manage those modes, the company said in a statement Thursday. Loadsure’s product allows shippers, freight brokers, or carriers to insure shipments instantly and on-demand. That allows those entities to adjust the level of insurance to account for changes in dynamics while cargo is in transit, while also giving entities with constrained access to insurance products the ability to tap into risk mitigation tools. Loadsure said in the statement it estimates 60 to 90 percent of cargo in transit is underinsured or uninsured, “in part because traditional insurance can’t keep pace with the just-in-time supply chain.” With Thursday’s round, Loadsure, founded in 2018, has now raised $12.4 million, including a seed round of financing in March 2020. Founder and CEO Johnny McCord said in the statement that the company will use the funding to make strategic hires and expand the business, particularly to sell its services to brokers and forwarders. The company is also used by traditional channels such as insurance brokers and wholesalers. Loadsure’s product can be used in a standalone fashion or through an embedded application programming interface (API) through which intermediaries can offer their customers insurance at the time of a transaction. Its existing broker, software, and freight marketplace partners include Redwood Logistics, Trucker Tools, Emerge, DAT Freight & Analytics, Kleinschmidt, and Cargo Chief. The basic premise is to make insurance quoting, claims submission, settlement, and payment more efficient through a purely digital process. The company leans on a machine learning model to base risk assessments for its underwriting decisions. Massimo Messina, Crowley’s vice president of mergers and acquisitions, said in a separate statement Thursday that its investment was aimed at meeting “the growing need for cost-effective risk management.” Loadsure’s round was led by London-based early stage venture investor MMC Ventures, with existing investor Insuretech Gateway participating alongside Crowley. title: Forwarding tech provider out to unify disconnected system landscape
content: Prompt founder Robert Petti previously led a business intelligence initiative at Toll Global Forwarding before working to ease access to such tools for smaller forwarders. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A data entry and integration automation software vendor that has been quietly working with a range of the biggest global forwarders said Monday it is extending the range of logistics solutions into which it integrates. New York-based Prompt essentially provides a workflow layer on top of widely used logistics systems for forwarders and logistics operators, with a customer list that includes DSV, Toll Global Forwarding, CEVA Logistics, and Crowley Maritime. The company has largely operated in stealth since its founding in 2020. The company started by providing that layer specifically for users of WiseTech Global’s CargoWise system, a transportation management and operations system with more than 18,000 global customers, including 42 of the top 50 global third-party logistics providers (3PLs). But Prompt is expanding its integrations to other commonly used forwarder platforms, including BluJay Solutions (now a part of E2open), Magaya, and SAP. Its product suite primarily addresses data capture, freight audit and pay, customer visibility, management analytics, rate management, and payment processing, founder Robert Petti told JOC.com. Petti added that the software is aimed at expanding the functionality of a transportation management system (TMS) without changing or replacing any of a forwarder’s existing software. Interest in the product has accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic as forwarders wrestle with increased cargo volume and revenue growth during a time when labor to support that growth is hard to find, he said. Petti set out to build Prompt based initially on his experience building business intelligence (BI) capability at Toll nearly a decade ago. In 2015, he founded a company called Lading to create a BI layer to run on forwarding systems. “To me, it was silly that only big companies with six- and seven-figure budgets had good BI reporting,” Petti said. He set out to build a software-as-a-service (SaaS) layer for BI, but admitted his idea was “way too early” and instead became a platinum CargoWise Service Partner, a designation that alludes to its preferred status to help with forwarding solutions, integrations, workflow, and accounting. That arrangement ended in 2020, which enabled Petti to start Prompt and work with other systems. “We wanted the optionality we didn’t have with exclusive arrangement,” he said. “A lot of companies use CargoWise for customs and Magaya for warehousing, as an example. Why not allow them to operate out of an aggregated layer? That’s a big goal.” Aside from the broader ambition of helping forwarders to stitch together products from multiple systems, Prompt is focused on better use of single systems, too. “All the [forwarder] TMSs are good, but they all have gaps,” Petti said. “We used to waste so much time manually entering data from documents into our TMS,” Spencer Hutchins, vice president of freight forwarding operations at Vantec Hitachi Transport Systems, said in a statement from Prompt. “A complex 200-page commercial invoice used to take one person five business days to capture into CargoWise. Now it takes 20 minutes.” Prompt also helps forwarders manage the merging of systems and databases as a result of acquisitions. “We needed a way to transfer data to CargoWise from a recent acquisition’s database, but we didn’t have time to get approval from IT for an integration build that would be scrapped after a few months anyway,” Bruno Tarikian, director of innovation services at DSV, said in the statement. The ability tap into multiple systems through a single enterprise window and enable critical capabilities through a single provider is ultimately where Prompt sees itself achieving broader traction. “One integration to Prompt allows us to deliver a set of critical capabilities and brings information across systems together for users,” company COO Kai Timmerman told JOC.com. “Connecting to any of the top company’s tech stack is a multi-month process,” Petti added. “Why go to only an freight audit and pay, or a rate management product, if they can get it all through one integration?” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Supply chains top CFO business risk concerns
content: Supply chain disruptions pose the biggest business risk this year, cited by 84% of CFOs in a BDO survey of 600 finance leaders at companies with annual sales of between $500 million and $3 billion. “The pandemic exposed weaknesses in global supply chains, [but] these issues were percolating well before,” the survey report says. Talent shortages and the potential for tax law changes are other top risks. COVID-19, on the other hand, is receding as a priority, although the change in how people work because of the pandemic has heightened cybersecurity risks. Almost 80% of CFOs in the survey cite data privacy breaches as a top risk this year, a concern validated by an Accenture report released last week that found ransomware attacks were up 107% in 2021 compared with 2020. “Cloud [computing] plays into ransomware’s hands,” Accenture said. “Cloud environments were and continue to be attractive targets, perhaps due to lower monitoring levels than on-premise environments.” Supply chain risks are multifaceted and inter-connected, the BDO survey finds. CFOs cite rising material and transportation costs along with delays and shortages among their top supply-side concerns while worrying about customer preferences on the demand side. “People want and expect same-day shipping,” the report says. “It’s no wonder supply chains are CFOs’ biggest headache.” To keep costs down and meet those high customer expectations, CFOs call accurate demand and inventory management their most important supply chain priority. The goal is to leverage technology to replace the just-in-time inventory approach that has been causing bottlenecks this past year with something similarly cost-effective but more resilient. “Just-in-time … was never intended to be implemented without building in any redundancy — but in many cases, keeping costs low took precedence,” the report says. CarParts.com, a big seller of gaskets, brakes and other products to consumers for do-it-yourself repairs, is holding far more inventory than it did pre-pandemic, part of the company’s plan to side-step shortages and delays to meet customers’ expectations. “In this environment [just-in-time] doesn’t work,” David Meniane, the company’s CFO, told CFO Dive. “The longer the lead time, the less reliable the supply chain, the more inventory you have to carry. Otherwise we lose the sale to whoever has inventory and is more aggressive.” It’s a costly solution. In the third quarter of last year, the company was holding almost $132 million in parts, three times more than it typically would pre-pandemic. But Meniane is counting on it being a temporary solution. His plan is to transition to something closer to just-in-time but with more resiliency built in. “As lead times compress, you’re going to see more firms having less inventory,” he said.

title: K+N taps startup to improve container import efficiency
content: Flowfox is already working with some of the largest container lines in the world to streamline import processes that are generally coordinated via email, CEO Patrick Pehmöller told JOC.com. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Kuehne + Nagel is working with Hamburg-based container logistics technology provider Flowfox to pilot the latter’s system that manages a range of import-related equipment and availability processes, the companies said Wednesday. Flowfox provides software to help container lines automate the coordination of container releases from terminals and re-use of import containers for export loads. Forwarders and consignees can use the platform for free to calculate real-time detention and demurrage costs, provide instructions about container deliver on carrier haulage moves — also known as door moves — and to convey changes to container pickups and dropoffs. Flowfox CEO Patrick Pehmöller told JOC.com the ambition of the company is to enable container lines to turn their import management departments from cost centers to profit centers by helping them move away from email as the coordinating platform. By doing so, he said, forwarders and shippers benefit through enhanced efficiency related to container availability status and the payments required to release a container. “The challenge is the manual processes,” he said. “Communication is done by email and there is no transparency. So there is no clarity about when is the container release done, has the bill of lading been surrendered, has the terminal accepted the release, is the container available?” Flowfox aims to make payment status, ancillary charges due, detention and demurrage costs, and other factors that constrain movement of containers more accessible to forwarders and shippers. “And then to make that transparent and payable for the consignee at any time either through our own solution or some other solution they already use,” Pehmöller said. Forwarders and shippers automatically get a digital bank account when they sign up to use Flowfox to make ACH payments to carriers and terminals. Those parties can also dictate when they want to pick up their containers and the delivery location, enabling carriers and terminals to better plan stacking operations in the terminal and sequence pickup appointments. The platform is also a place to coordinate re-use of container, known as street turns or matchbacks. That helps export shippers find equipment, and reduces the empty return burden on import shippers, but it also helps container lines better utilize their assets, Pehmöller said. Founded in 2019, Flowfox already works with some of the largest container lines in the world, Pehmöller said. The pilot with K+N is aimed at helping the German global forwarder coordinate container availability, as well as container release and re-use with the carriers it uses. “We see huge potential to largely automate the import processes with our ocean carrier partners and we are now starting to pilot the Flowfox platform in Europe with major ocean carriers with the aim to roll out the solution globally,” Markus Johannsen, senior vice president/global seafreight and global head of operations/sea logistics for K+N, said in a statement. Flowfox said in the statement it received an undisclosed amount of funding from investors in December, and that the cash has been used to build its development team and add sales representatives in Europe and Asia. title: One solution to the congestion problem: More inland ports
content: One of the lessons that supply chain stakeholders have learned during the COVID-19 pandemic is the vital role inland ports play in fighting congestion. But what measures should be taken to fully utilize existing ports? Can — and should — new inland ports be developed? And what role can the railroads play in that? FreightWaves spoke with three supply chain experts to get their thoughts. Congestion not only at the West Coast ports but also at inland hubs such as Chicago the past two years has made all stakeholders zero in on improving coordination along the supply chain. “Imagine there’s a big movie theater, and you’re trying to exit out of a very small door. There’s just no solution that will help out when there’s that much volume but no coordination in trying to get out,” said Steve Wen, CEO of Dray Alliance, a software company that connects shippers with networks of drayage carriers. “So, either we need to have a more data-driven method of planning how things get in and out, or there should be another exit, which is the inland port idea.” Indeed, stakeholders have realized that the supply chain needs to change to accommodate growing consumer demand and the e-commerce boom. “As you look at e-commerce and how that’s evolving, it implies that you’re trying to get your inventory closer to the customer,” said Mark Yeager, CEO for 3PL Redwood Logistics. “What that means is using multiple midmarket cities as points of distribution, as opposed to [using] Chicago or Atlanta.” One way to accommodate that is through better utilization of inland ports. Also known as dry ports, these sites provide inland shippers with typically rail access to coastal ports. Inland ports also allow the loading of ship cargo and imports onto trains at coastal ports. The cargo is then hauled to the inland ports, which may be hundreds of miles from congested coastal ports, for unloading and further distribution. Inland ports could help create capacity at coastal ports by offering more slack to the overall system, Wen said. Inland ports could also relieve physical and regulatory constraints that some coastal ports, such as the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach in California, face in building out port infrastructure. Everybody wants to ramp up capacity. It’s just the matching of the demand and supply sides that is the difficult part, because the demand side doesn’t always know what capacity is available, while the supply side doesn’t always know where the demand is,” Lew said. “Shippers need to be more proactive about approaching logistics providers, terminal operators, short lines, railroads about what they want, and let the supply side try to come up with solutions that can solve the problem,” Lew said. “But that collaboration is something that needs to be more proactively done. And not done just when there’s an emergency … . That collaboration is something that I think needs to be done much more in advance.” Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inbox. title: ‘Hell on wheels’: CP rail shutdown brings more pain to supply chain
content: Two days after Canadian Pacific Railway shut down its rail network amid a labor dispute with more than 3,000 of its Teamsters-represented employees, the impacts to the supply chain are just getting started. The loss of Canada’s second-largest freight rail operator has stalled shipments of everything from grain to containers full of electronics headed to cities across Canada and the U.S. And it will soon inevitably bring backups to ports, including Vancouver, British Columbia, and Montreal. “This is hell on wheels,” said Manny Calandrino, president and CEO of Consolidated Fastfrate, a Toronto-area-based LTL carrier that has long-standing partnership with CP and is co-located at its intermodal facilities in Canada. As of Monday evening, CP and Teamsters Canada Rail Conference remained in talks with federal mediators. Engineers, conductors and yard workers picketed outside CP rail facilities across Canada. Apart from the underlying contract dispute over pay and pensions, the two sides are also at odds over whether CP locked out the 3,000 workers or the union began a strike early Sunday. CP and Teamsters Canada declined to comment on the impacts of the rail network shut down. A spokesperson for CP said the company “remains at the table.” In Canada, CP’s rail network stretches from Vancouver to Montreal, and in the U.S. it reaches key U.S. markets including Chicago, New York and Minneapolis. The railroad also provides an essential link to the ports of Vancouver and Montreal — Canada’s busiest — through on-dock access. Both the Vancouver and Montreal port authorities said they are continuing to monitor the situation. The consequences of disrupting those rail links with the ports can quickly cascade into something larger. In December, landslides cut off CN and CP’s main lines serving Vancouver. At one point 60 ships were waiting to dock in Vancouver as a result. While just CP is affected, the current disruption is playing out over a much wider swath of the supply chain. And there are simply no relief valves. “You only have a matter of days, if not hours, before you have a landlocked and bottlenecked supply chain on top of everything else that has been contributing to the quagmire over the past several years,” said Julia Kuzeljevich, spokesperson for the Canadian International Freight Forwarders Association. Calandrino said his customers are left with few options, since there’s little capacity on CN’s rails. Some are willing to pay rates of four to five times those of rail to have freight moved by truck, which Fastfrate contracts out. But many aren’t. “They’re going to try holding it for a bit on their own, in their own warehouses, and not ship until this is over,” he said. “But that leads to more delays.” The shutdown adds to a long list of disruptions. There was the blockade of the busiest commercial border between the Ambassador Bridge in February, the landslides in British Columbia in December and the Montreal port strike in April. “We really didn’t need this one,” Calandrino said. Before COVID, in November 2019, CN rail workers went on a weeklong strike. In that case, CN and the Teamsters Canada Rail Conference reached an agreement. But it’s not clear what will happen this time. There have already been calls from multiple industry groups to legislate the CP workers back to work. Canadian labor law expert Sara Slinn, a professor at Osgoode Hall Law School at York University, said there is a “very good likelihood that the government will entertain back-to-work legislation” because of the ongoing strains in the supply chain, and fears over commodity shortages because of the war in Ukraine. “Supply chain disruptions and price problems and inflation and scarcity have been the forefront of the news for a long, long time and really blew up with those more recent events,” she said. For now, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s minister of labor, Seamus O’Regan, is continuing to urge CP and the Teamsters to hash things out. “We have faith in their ability to reach an agreement,” O’Regan said in a statement. “Canadians expect them to do that ASAP.” Click for more FreightWaves articles by Nate Tabak Past the hype. title: FMC probing major liners, ‘pop-up’ carriers on US export service
content: The FMC alleges that small, independent ocean carriers are neglecting US exporters in favor of returning empty containers to China. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) will audit 16 ocean carriers in two separate actions involving their US export business, a group that includes what the FMC called five “pop-up” carriers that have emerged in the trans-Pacific market of late in response to surging import demand. The scrutiny on export capacity availability comes as the US trade deficit reaches a 14-year high, the agency said. It also comes as US shippers, particularly those involved in exporting agricultural goods, have alleged that ocean carriers are unfairly denying them export containers in favor of returning empty boxes back to Asia so they can be quickly reloaded with more lucrative US imports. The FMC said Monday an upcoming round of meetings it will have will focus on 11 major carriers. Those carriers are: CMA CGM, Cosco Shipping, Evergreen Marine, Hapag-Lloyd, HMM, Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Co., Ocean Network Express (ONE), Yang Ming, OOCL, and Zim Shipping, the FMC said. The audits are part of the FMC’s ongoing investigation that started in July 2021 into the various fees that ocean carriers charge shippers for the usage of containers. The FMC said they will cover market trends and service performance, but also look for areas where “opportunities exist for individual lines to improve or increase access to service offerings,” the FMC said in a statement. In addition to those meetings, the FMC said its Bureau of Enforcement is separately examining five independent container lines about how they too are serving US exporters. Those carriers are BAL Container Line, CULines, Lihua Logistics Company, Transfar Shipping, and X-Press Container Line, the FMC said in a statement to JOC.com. Over the last 12 months, those carriers have added services to both the US West Coast and East Coast thanks to the strong demand from US importers. The review will look at all the vessel calls the five carriers have made to the US since June 2021 and include data on the number of loaded and empty containers the carriers are bringing back to Asia. FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said the five independent carriers have the same legal obligations under the US Shipping Act as do major carriers. “New entrants to the market — including the so-called pop-up carriers — have all the same responsibilities as companies that have served the U.S. trades for decades,” Maffei said in the statement. In a separate statement, FMC Commissioner Carl Bentzel said that during a recent visit to the Port of Long Beach, his observations about the business practices of independent carriers suggests that they only provide a one-way service from China, with little emphasis on serving US exporters. He added that the Shipping Act of 1984 offers protections to exporters in instances where carriers “unreasonably refuse to deal or negotiate” for capacity. “Accordingly, my observations concerning ‘one-way’ service remain and I continue to express concerns that these carriers could be behaving in a manner that violates common carriage protections of the law,” Bentzel said. title: Just 3 years after 2019’s trucking bloodbath, another is on the way
content: After two years of COVID-induced havoc in global freight markets, volatility has started to abate. FreightWaves’ view of the market has become clearer, and the picture isn’t pretty. We think another sharp, painful downturn in the U.S. truckload market is imminent, and it could be as bad as 2019. March has been unusually soft in the truckload freight market, according to the SONAR Outbound Tender Volume Index (OTVI). Because this index measures actual truckload tenders in the contract market, it provides a very reliable indicator of market direction. March is typically a strong month for trucking, as shippers start to stock their shelves in preparation for summer. And late March normally gets a reliable end-of-quarter boost in volumes as shippers pump sales and reduce inventories. This year, we are not seeing that surge. In fact, March volumes are softer than at any point in 2021 (other than holidays). The OTVI (in blue) is currently sitting at 13,571. It was 15,531 at the end of January and 15,859 a year ago. The orange line is 2021. More than likely, the lower volumes are due to a major consumer slowdown. Inflation that began in 2020, combined with the surge in fuel prices related to increased inflation and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, have made consumers move to the sidelines. Back in 2019, FreightWaves reporters wrote about trucking bankruptcies almost every day. I expect this will become reality for us once again. Past the hype. title: BlueX tackles freight cost burden with ‘pay-it-later’ tool
content: BlueX last month launched an electronic payment platform for entities in the liner shipping industry designed to speed payment across borders. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Ocean freight software provider BlueX Trade has expanded its recently launched payment solution to enable small shippers to get access to extended credit terms to cover volatile freight and ancillary costs. The product, BlueX Pay-it-Later, is an extension of BlueX Pay, an electronic platform aimed at helping speed payments between forwarders, container lines, terminals, and shippers, the company said in a statement Thursday. The new product is essentially a financing tool to allow small shippers or forwarders struggling with supply chain disruption to ease cashflow pressure tied to freight costs. Pay-it-Later is also meant to help shippers and forwarders expedite cargo release in situations where the cost to release cargo from a terminal ties up working capital. “The rising costs of our shipping are more manageable” with the financing product, Josephine Huang, president of Soho Kitchen Studio, a Southern California-based kitchen design and construction company and a BlueX customer, said in the statement. “It’s a game-changer for any business struggling with the rising freight costs." The product provides qualified small businesses with access to funds to pay ocean freight, demurrage, detention, and other gate fees with 30- to 60-day credit terms. For those companies needing expedited cargo release, BlueX combines Pay-it-Later with an expedited payment to carriers and 50 North American marine terminals. “The current volatility and high logistics costs in the market are challenging small and medium-sized shippers who want to grow their business,” BlueX Trade CEO Sean O’Malley said in the statement. Freight payment and financing technology is quickly becoming a competitive battleground in the logistics industry, with standalone payment platforms such as PayCargo and Melio, and even forwarders themselves, aiming to arm payers with more efficient payment tools. Shifl, a New York-based forwarder, launched a payment tool in January to aimed at helping shippers clear cargo faster. On the financing side, options for small shippers are growing as well. New York-based startup Fishtail, for example, announced a $4.5 million round to build its freight and trade finance platform earlier this week. BlueX, founded in 2018 with offices in San Francisco and Taiwan, started out building digital commerce tools for container lines, including Evergreen Line and Yang Ming, before branching out into payment and finance tools. title: Shippers resume complaints to FMC over unfulfilled contract space
content: Complaints made to the FMC contend that container lines intentionally sold capacity on the more lucrative spot market in lieu of providing the allocated space to shippers on lower contract rate levels. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Shippers are increasingly turning to the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to seek relief in disputes with container lines and marine terminals, with three more formal complaints filed this month. Two container lines intentionally refused contract rate bookings to chase higher spot market rates, according to allegations made in complaints filed March 8 and 18, respectively. A third complaint, filed March 21, alleges a Port of Long Beach container terminal assessed excessive demurrage fees on a shipment in the fall of 2020. The latest complaints reflect a frustrated shipper community increasingly more willing to take their disputes to regulators. A July complaint by a Pennsylvania-based home goods importer was the first formal complaint accusing container lines of taking advantage of pandemic-driven disruption in ways that violate the US Shipping Act. The sides eventually settled, but more shippers have since filed complaints. A March 18 filing by New Jersey-based Foreign Tire Sales (FTS) against Evergreen Shipping Agency demonstrates that growing frustration. “Evergreen advised FTS and its vendors that there was no space in ships bound for the USA and then turned around and gave the space that should have been given to FTS to non-vessel operators (NVOs) at much higher rates than the rates promised in the contract between FTS and Evergreen,” the shipper said in its complaint. The impact of Evergreen not honoring its contract was higher ocean freight costs for FTS, with the shipper needing to turn to NVOs to secure capacity for its goods, it said. “The difference between the rates that Evergreen agreed to are up to $15,000 per container less than rates charged by NVOs,” FTS said in the complaint. In the first case, submitted March 8, Houston-based importer Royal White Cement (RWC) said CMA CGM refused to honor bookings made under a contract, signed May 11, 2021, for service between the Egyptian ports of Said and Damietta and the US through April 30, 2022. The shipper alleges CMA CGM did so in order to sell that capacity on the more lucrative spot market. The contract committed RWC to move 1,000 containers during the year, but it alleges CMA CGM stopped accepting bookings attached to its contract rate after 10 containers. It moved 2,843 containers in its previous annual contract, 1,343 more than its minimum quantity commitment (MQC) specified, the filing said. The cases are the first to be filed with the FMC since Jan. 19, reigniting complaints from shippers seeking help from the FMC to resolve cases where shippers allege container lines are not fulfilling the annual MQCs to which they contractually agreed. The FMC in December invited shippers to submit complaints as part of a stronger remit to regulate the market as ocean freight rates skyrocketed in 2021. Prior to that, the Commission agreed on a policy to prohibit carrier retaliation against shippers that filed complaints. The FMC has also taken a harder line on carrier and terminal assessment of detention and demurrage. The demurrage complaint, filed by California-based ACME Freight Services against Total Terminals International, alleges that a shipment of several boxes that were part of a consignment of 20 containers of medical gloves incurred more than $185,000 worth of demurrage due to a hold by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). The logistics provider contends it was not responsible for the customs hold, which was related to another logistics company and different container line, and therefore should not be held responsible for demurrage related to the hold. title: Tracking the air cargo industry's response to Russia's war on Ukraine
content: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has added another obstacle for air cargo-reliant supply chains already challenged by climbing rates and limited capacity. Airlines large and small have adjusted their operations to minimize the war’s impact, leading many to cancel services and flights to Ukraine and Russia as early as Feb. 24, when the attack began. The two countries are also home to fleets that specialize in handling extra-large cargo, which are hard to find elsewhere. Commercial flights have vanished from the skies of Ukraine and surrounding areas as carriers avoid the conflict’s airspace. Rerouted flights and climbing fuel costs have resulted in higher surcharges for shippers and further flight cancellations as some services between Europe and Asia became economically unviable for carriers. This has happened during a period of already limited cargo space, as the COVID-19 pandemic grounded many aircraft due to plummeting passenger demand. “With the crisis in Ukraine now, we’re sort of back to those early days of the pandemic because lots of capacity has been sidelined,” Neel Jones Shah, Flexport’s executive vice president and global head of airfreight, said earlier this month. Some air cargo carriers are still traveling freely through Russian airspace. Airplanes for China Southern and Air China were doing so on Wednesday afternoon, per Flightradar24. But at least 11 of the world’s top 25 cargo airlines, according to the International Air Transport Association’s (IATA) 2020 rankings, and smaller operators have made some sort of adjustment due to the war. Here is a rundown of those changes. Included in the list for most carriers is 2020 data from IATA on cargo tonne-kilometers (CTK) flown, a measure of cargo activity. This list will be updated regularly.

title: SEC proposes 'rules of the road' for climate risk disclosures
content: The SEC proposal will probably come under fire from industry groups claiming that the agency seeks to impose an excessive burden on companies and is ranging beyond its expertise and congressional mandate, according to attorneys who specialize in environmental law. The rules are now subject to a two-month public comment period. Organizations such as the Business Roundtable and U.S. Chamber of Commerce may challenge the SEC’s bedrock assertion that carbon emissions is a “material” fact that should be included on a company’s financial statements, David Brown at Alston & Bird told CFO Dive. Also, SEC “mission creep is absolutely a risk,” Brown said, spotlighting the requirement for third–party attestations of carbon emissions estimates and the mandate that some companies report on so-called Scope 3 emissions by their suppliers, vendors and other third parties across their supply chains. Such reports would be phased in, subject to safe harbor protections and not required of smaller companies. “CFOs should absolutely have their radar up for the additional costs and burdens that it would take in order to comply with this,” Brown said in an interview with CFO Dive. Compliance with the disclosure rules would “take a lot of growing pains,” he said, requiring greater spending on more in-house expertise and other resources. If enacted, the SEC proposal would speed the growth of a “climate industrial complex,” SEC Commissioner Hester Peirce said before voting against the disclosure requirements. “We are here laying the cornerstone of a new disclosure framework that will eventually rival our existing securities disclosure framework in magnitude and cost and probably outpace it in complexity.” “The proposal takes us outside of our statutory jurisdiction and expertise, which harms the agency’s integrity,” she said. “In addition, filling SEC filings with information that is inherently unreliable undercuts the credibility of the rest of the information in these important filings.” U.S. lawmakers and industry groups have said rules for detailed carbon emissions disclosure could increase companies’ litigation risk and raise their cost of capital. The 12 Republican senators on the Senate Banking Committee in a March 7 letter to Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen warned about “the potential damaging effects to national security from the unprecedented efforts of federal financial agencies to develop regulations that some intend to use for limiting U.S. energy producers’ access to credit and capital. “Such actions would begin to curtail the supply of domestic energy, leading to higher costs for American households and making our country and allies more vulnerable to the consequences of Russian aggression,” according to the senators, including Pat Toomey, R-Pa., the committee’s ranking member. Before enacting new climate-related regulation, the SEC should first consider U.S. energy security and “the threat to global energy supplies from Russia and similar repressive regimes,” the senators said. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce said Monday the agency proposal will not help efforts by companies to provide investors with useful climate risk information. The chamber “is concerned that the prescriptive approach taken by the SEC will limit companies’ ability to provide information that shareholders and stakeholders find meaningful while at the same time requiring that companies provide information in securities filings that are not material to investors,” according to Tom Quaadman, executive vice president for the chamber’s Center for Capital Markets Competitiveness. “The Supreme Court has been clear that any required disclosures under securities laws must meet the test of materiality, and we will advocate against provisions of this proposal that deviate from that standard or are unnecessarily broad,” Quaadman said in a statement. Environmental groups hailed the SEC proposal. “Investors need to understand the size and scope of climate risk, and today’s proposal is a welcome step toward that goal,” Michael Panfil, director of climate risk strategies for the Environmental Defense Fund told CFO Dive. “Climate-related financial risks are already significant and growing every day,” he said. “In the last two years alone, the United States has suffered from more than 40 weather and climate disasters that each caused at least $1 billion in economic damages.” Investors with $130 trillion in assets under management have pushed for climate risk disclosures, Gensler said before the SEC vote.

title: Subramaniam to lead FedEx into post-Smith era
content: There is opportunity for greater integration of FedEx Ground and Express within the US, a freight consultant says. Photo credit: FedEx Corp. The transition at the top of FedEx, with current COO and President Raj Subramaniam becoming CEO on June 1, paves the way for the next stage in the evolution of the global transportation and logistics provider, according to Satish Jindel, president of transportation research firm SJ Consulting Group. FedEx announced Monday that founder, chairman, and CEO Frederick W. Smith would become executive chairman when he steps aside in favor of Subramaniam. The next stage of the company’s evolution could include the integration of FedEx Express’s US operations and FedEx Ground, said Jindel, who helped found Roadway Package System, the predecessor company to FedEx Ground, in the 1980s. “Integration will enhance shareholder value, increase operating income, and help with the management of properties, package sortation, and linehaul optimization,” Jindel said in an interview with JOC.com Tuesday. Such an integration would leave FedEx looking more like its main competitor, UPS, at least in the US. “International will remain what it is, but domestically express and ground could be integrated,” said Jindel, who has also urged a spin-off of FedEx Freight that would make the largest US LTL trucking company a stand-alone entity. UPS last year sold its LTL subsidiary to TFI International. There’s already much unofficial integration taking place, with FedEx Ground assisting FedEx Express in US deliveries and FedEx Freight running linehaul trailers for FedEx Ground, Jindel said. Richard Smith, son of the founder, also is moving higher in the chain of command. The younger Smith, currently regional president for the Americas at FedEx Express, will become president and CEO-elect of the air express division April 1, taking full control of the division in September. FedEx Express’s current CEO, Donald F. Colleran, will become an executive advisor and then retire Dec. 31, FedEx announced separately on March 10. R. Brad Martin, chair of the audit committee of FedEx’s board of directors, is now non-executive vice chairman of the board, and has become the board’s designated successor to serve as chairman when Smith becomes executive chairman, FedEx also announced Monday. Subramaniam takes charge as FedEx deals with a global surge in e-commerce and challenges to the system of global free trade that helped Smith build the company. Over five decades, Smith has been a forceful advocate for free trade, championing FedEx’s role in promoting economic growth and prosperity in a keynote speech at JOC’s 2014 TPM Conference in Long Beach, California. “Over the last few years, almost every trading nation has introduced policies that permit greater government intervention in the trade process,” Smith said at TPM 2014. The trend he noted then has only grown in recent years, with the US-China trade war and the Russian invasion of Ukraine and its resultant sanctions pushing nations toward trading blocs at a rate not seen since the 1970s. FedEx revenue rose 10 percent in its last fiscal quarter to $23.6 billion. Investments in its network have positioned the company to compete more aggressively in global e-commerce, Subramaniam said in a conference call with analysts March 17. “We are focused on getting revenue quality, making sure we put the right package in the right network,” whether air or ground, he said. title: Retail boss warns on supply chain, likens demand risk to ‘Big Short’
content: Some quarterly calls by public companies are basically worthless, featuring analysts lobbing softball questions to CEOs who cherry-pick facts to pump their own stock. And then there was Tuesday afternoon’s call hosted by Gary Friedman, CEO of luxury home furnishings brand RH (NYSE: RH), formerly known as Restoration Hardware. Friedman — with what one analyst called “brutal honesty” — expounded upon supply chain woes, surging ocean freight rates, soaring inflation and a sudden plunge in consumer demand coinciding with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “I’m just going to tell the truth,” he said. “Maybe our stock is going to take a big hit because of this.” He was right. His company’s market value fell by $1 billion on Wednesday. “Everybody thinks supply chains are getting better. I don’t think they’ve gotten better at all,” Friedman said. “Product is on the water for a long time, getting ships into port. We’ve got about five extra weeks in our supply chain right now. That’s a lot of time, a lot of money. And that’s the average. Some stuff’s coming on time and some is 10-12 weeks behind. “Many of us thought we’d have been caught up by now. We’ll be lucky to be caught up by the end of the year,” he said, pointing to heavy omicron impacts on supply chains in China, Vietnam and other sourcing countries. “It’s hitting everybody from all angles. You just have this compounding supply chain kind of puzzle happening. “I’ve never seen it so chaotic, honestly, from a [project] execution point of view, whether it’s construction, sourcing, manufacturing, shifting supply chains or freight. Everything is a little out of sync in the world right now.” On freight pricing, Friedman pointed out that most U.S. importers have already signed annual trans-Pacific contracts for 2022. “I wonder if anybody at the Fed has picked up the phone and called a businessperson and said, ‘Hey, what do you think is happening with inflation? How are ocean rates?” He disclosed that after the initial supply chain disruption in 2020, RH’s average freight rate doubled from $2,400 to $4,800 per forty-foot equivalent unit. “I’m not going to tell you what it just went to. But let’s just say that [earlier doubling] looks like a nice increase [in comparison]. And it’s not just us. It’s everybody.” The biggest revelation on the RH call was Friedman’s disclosure on demand. He revealed that the company saw a 10-12% drop in demand “overnight” coinciding with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine — and no recovery since then. “Other people might be banging a brighter, happier drum than me. Do they have better numbers than we do? I don’t think so.” He noted that most other U.S. retailers reported earlier than RH and had focused disclosures on Q1 sales, not current demand. RH’s Q1 sales will be strong too, he pointed out, courtesy of the backlog built up before the drop. “I think we’re the first ones talking about demand,” he said. “The invasion of Ukraine by Russia just became kind of a reckoning point. People had to stop and pay attention to everything. And I don’t think it’s all about Ukraine and Russia. I think it triggered a greater awareness. It was like: Ring the bell, everybody pay attention” — not just to the war itself, but to the prewar surge in inflation, the Fed’s decision to hike interest rates, overheating in real estate and other concerns. “I don’t want to scare everybody,” he said. He proceeded to say something scary, likening the recent shift in conditions to the scene in the financial-crisis movie “The Big Short” when a conference panelist was told, “From the time you guys started talking, Bear Stearns’ stock has fallen by more than 38%,” and attendees frantically checked their Blackberrys and scrambled from the room even though Alan Greenspan was the next scheduled speaker. “Everything is kind of happening at once,” said Friedman, who cited consequences for both retail sales timing and product pricing. Asked by an analyst whether supply chain issues would affect the launch of RH’s Contemporary-branded collection, Friedman laughed and responded: “What do you think? Of course.” That catalog was supposed to go out in March. It will go out in May instead because “we want to have some goods in stock,” he said. The catalog will be cut from 450-500 pages to 300-350 pages because “stuff is late and my sense is it might even be later.” He also confirmed that RH will be passing along its higher costs to consumers. “When you have this kind of impact from freight and raw materials and price increases from suppliers and so on, you can say, ‘Oh, we’re big. We can absorb it.’ But that’s kind of BS. What’s happening in the world today is prices are going up everywhere. If they’re not, earnings are going to go down. “The question people have to ask is: ‘Do I want to be a bigger, lower-margin business and chase sales? Or do I want to be a smaller, higher-margin business and come out of this really positioned for the long term?’ And that [higher-margin option] is the view we’ve taken.” The “Big Short”-esque risk ahead is that higher costs (including container shipping freight) are passed along to consumers, the war stokes even higher inflation as it simultaneously curbs sentiment, the Fed proceeds with an extended run of rate hikes, and goods buying suffers for an extended period. According to Friedman, “I don’t think anybody really understands what’s coming from an inflation point of view, because either businesses are going to make a lot less money or they’re going to raise their prices. I don’t think anybody really understands how high prices are going to go. I think it’s going to outrun the consumer.” Past the hype. title: Easing container, truck rates bring cold comfort to US shippers
content: Asia–US West Coast container spot rates, as measured by Drewry, had fallen 11 percent by late March from Lunar New Year. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The slight easing of eastbound trans-Pacific container spot rates and US truckload spot rates, coupled with weakening economic indicators, is dangling signs of so-called normalization for ocean and surface transport prices. That those record highs may be over will be cold comfort for shippers, however. Container lines are hedging any comments on the easing of container rates and US port congestion with warnings that the volume pressure isn’t letting up and port performance gains may slip again. Zim Integrated Shipping Services, for example, told investors it expected some spot rate normalization in the second half of this year. Yet the carrier’s leadership told JOC.com nothing was guaranteed. “It is possible there will be actually no [container spot rate] normalization before 2023,” Xavier Destriau, Zim’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, said March 9. “There is no significant capacity coming in 2022 and incremental capacity will only start coming in 2023.” OOCL was also hesitant to say when spot rates might ease, telling investors on March 25 that it “does not expect such high freight rates are sustainable in the medium to long term.” Container freight rates generally dip after the Chinese New Year, and this year was no different, although the decline was less than in the last five years, Jeremy Nixon, CEO of Ocean Network Express (ONE) said March 23. Asia–US West Coast container spot rates, as measured by Drewry, had fallen 11 percent by late March from Lunar New Year, although that was less than the approximately 18 percent decline seen in recent years for the time period, according to maritime analyst Lars Jensen. At slightly less than $10,000 per FEU, spot rates on the eastbound trans-Pacific are still up 130 percent from a year ago. On the surface side, weighted truckload rates quoted by brokers to shippers peaked in November, according to DAT Freight & Analytics. But market volatility and higher fuel prices are keeping rates elevated even if they are off their late 2021 highs. Since the weighted average rate per mile for dry truckloads hit $4.37 per mile in January, pricing has declined each month, with average weighted rates falling to $3.46 per mile in March. Rising prices for staples such as food and gasoline and other inflationary pressures are sapping US consumer confidence in the short-term. Although US consumer confidence in March rebounded marginally, America’s optimism for the coming months when it comes to income, business, and labor conditions has darkened. The index fell from 80.8 in February to 76.6 in March, according to the latest reading of The Conference Board’s Consumer Confidence Index. Consumer sentiment for the short-term “has weakened further with consumers citing rising prices, especially at the gas pump, and the war in Ukraine as factors,” Lynn Franco, senior director of economic indicators at The Conference Board. “Meanwhile, purchasing intentions for big-ticket items like automobiles have softened somewhat over the past few months as expectations for interest rates have risen.” US consumer inflation will rise 6.2 percent this year, compared with a 4.4 percent expansion last year, IHS Markit, now part of S&P Global, said in a March 18 report. Rising commodities prices and weaker stock prices will discourage personal consumption, with the impact of the war in Ukraine set to hit Americans hardest in the second and third quarters, according to IHS Markit. “Retail sales aren’t matching what companies expected just eight weeks ago,” said Paul Bingham, director of transportation consulting at IHS Markit. “We’re not going into a recession, but the composition of consumer spending will be different.” For now, US retailers are signaling they expect strong demand, projecting year-over-year increases in US imports in April, June, and July, according to Global Port Tracker, published by the National Retail Federation (NRF) and Hackett Associates. The NRF expects retail sales to expand 6 to 8 percent this year, compared with a 14 percent jump last year. Whether US ports are making progress in digging out of 21 months of record and near-record imports from Asia is a mixed bag. The South Carolina Ports Authority, for example, told The Journal of Commerce it can no longer give a timetable on when it will clear its backlog, which stood at 14 ships as of March 30 after swinging to two dozen earlier in the month, saying too many factors are beyond its control. As of March 29, the ship backlog in Southern California was below 50, but marine terminals tell JOC.com they expect the backlog to build again as ships delayed in Southern China due to COVID-19 restrictions join the queue off Los Angeles and Long Beach. ONE’s Nixon said he’d seen some improvement in port congestion on the US West Coast during port visits in early March, “but there was still a long way to go.” The easing of trans-Pacific spot rates is on a seemingly parallel journey.
