title: Top US Shippers: COVID-19 lockdowns, port congestion hampering US ag exports
content: Agricultural exports fell 10.4 percent in 2021, with major markets in Asia unlikely to bounce back quickly. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Despite forecasts for another strong harvest, US agricultural interests expect exports to decline for a second consecutive year in 2022 due to pandemic-related supply chain disruptions in Asia and continued congestion at major US ports and inland rail hubs. Extended COVID-19 lockdowns, particularly in China, have severely restricted labor availability and cargo movement among suppliers, factories, and ports throughout Asia, compromising the ability of textile and apparel producers to receive and process cotton imports, according to William Allen, president of the American Cotton Shippers Association. “All of the [Asian] markets are affected by COVID. The Chinese market is acutely affected by COVID,” Allen said, noting that those disruptions are expected to continue in the 2022–23 marketing year, which for most agricultural products begins in the fall. US containerized agricultural exports dropped 10.4 percent to 1.5 million TEU in 2021, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com within IHS Markit, now part of S&P Global. Asia remains by far the largest export market for US farmers, accounting for 71.6 percent of total agricultural exports last year, down slightly from 71.8 percent in 2020. US agricultural exports to North Asia — i.e., mainland China, Japan, Taiwan, and Korea — fell 6 percent in 2021, while exports to Southeast Asia tumbled 22.9 percent. Mike Steenhoek, executive director of the Soybean Transportation Coalition, said shortages of labor and containers and inland transportation bottlenecks in the US — all attributable to the nearly two-year deluge of consumer goods imports from Asia — have also restrained agricultural exports. Shipments of soybeans, hay, and cotton, which together comprise 62 percent of US agricultural exports, fell a combined 10.1 percent last year following a 20.2 percent increase in 2020. Because they are grown and harvested in the interior of the US, shippers of those commodities rely on a steady supply of empty containers and railroad capacity to get their products to the ports and, in turn, overseas markets. Steenhoek compared the agricultural supply chain with a relay race that is predicated on reliable baton handoffs between legs. “What happens if the runner is limping, or jogging, or has fallen and can’t get up at all? We need this predictability,” Steenhoek said. Agricultural exporters continue to experience difficulties in securing empty marine containers, erratic intermodal rail service, poor vessel schedule reliability, and port congestion and drayage issues in Asia. US exporters have accused carriers of deliberately limiting export bookings and equipment availability throughout the COVID-19 pandemic to return empty containers to Asia and refill them with more profitable merchandise imports. “There clearly is real frustration among exporters,” Steenhoek said. Soybean shippers’ description of their logistical problems range from “dire” to “it’s a problem, although I’m still exporting,” but responses from coalition members have been universally negative, he said. That frustration grew so intense that federal lawmakers are on the verge of enacting new legislation that would expand the oversight of the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to include, among other things, enforcement of so-called common carriage responsibilities. Currently in conference between the two chambers of Congress, the Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA) of 2022 would allow the FMC to refine and enforce rules governing the “reasonable” refusal of service to US exporters. Although they are supportive of those regulatory efforts, agricultural shippers concede they cannot prove in all instances that carriers’ refusal to carry certain export loads represents an unreasonable or discriminatory practice, Steenhoek said. For exporters able to secure bookings and equipment, unreliable vessel schedules and resulting changes to the earliest return date (ERD) — the window in which containers must be dropped off at marine terminals — have been especially damaging. Due to terminal congestion that has caused chronic vessel backups outside major US ports in 2021 and early 2022, carriers have been making frequent “live changes” to export ERDs that result in delays and added costs for exporters, Allen said. Those issues have been particularly acute at West Coast ports, which handle approximately one-third of US agricultural exports, but gateways on the East and Gulf coasts have also been grappling with vessel bunching as import containers stack up at marine terminals. What’s more, port officials expect congestion and vessel schedule disruptions to continue through 2022 despite a temporary slowing of volumes due to COVID-19 lockdowns in China. The queue of vessels waiting to berth in Los Angeles and Long Beach will likely increase again as already-arriving back-to-school merchandise collides with early peak season goods and an anticipated spike in imports once those lockdowns are lifted, Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, told a virtual press conference in mid-April. “We expect a pretty quick recovery [in volumes],” Seroka said. Griff Lynch, CEO of the Georgia Ports Authority, gave a similar prediction for conditions at the major East Coast gateways. “We fully anticipate vessels to backlog on the East Coast this summer,” Lynch told JOC.com. Global demand for high-quality US cotton remains strong, but to capitalize on that demand, shippers will need to work more closely with their logistics providers to secure capacity and equipment, avoid bottlenecks, and improve shipment visibility to increase speed to market, Allen said. “We are highly focused on executing the timely delivery of our product,” he said. title: project44, FourKites head of visibility class: Gartner
content: The report, which focused on trucking visibility, noted that most vendors are still dependent on customers and carrier connectivity in a limited set of regions. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A much-anticipated — and controversy-tinged — report by technology analyst Gartner on the state of the real-time transportation visibility (RTTV) market singled out two well-capitalized standalone visibility providers, project44 and FourKites, as leaders in the space. The report, called the Real-Time Transportation Visibility Provider Magic Quadrant (MQ), comes at a time when demand for predictive visibility tools has grown due to global supply chain disruptions that have made product lead times longer and less predictable. The controversy surrounding this year’s report — the second MQ that Gartner has issued on the visibility space — is tied to former Gartner vice president Bart de Muynck leaving the company to join project44 in mid-April. De Muynck was a lead author of the 2021 visibility report, but played no direct role in compiling this year’s version, Gartner said, although he did attend some vendor briefings in advance of the production of the report. The report rates 11 vendors, a mixture of pure-play visibility providers and visibility products attached to larger product suites that include transportation management, control tower, or supply chain planning capabilities. Gartner Research Director Carly West, the report’s author, noted that it sought to contextualize vendors that met certain thresholds for revenue, customer counts, geographic coverage, and business growth. While the report takes into account multimodal capability, it “represents a part of the end-to-end supply chain visibility market that predominantly — but not solely — addresses the domestic road transportation modes.” A number of vendors, who all asked not to be identified, reached out to JOC.com over the past week to voice concerns about the legitimacy of the report given de Muynck’s move to project44. The report was released May 24 to Gartner clients, but made more widely available this week. Gartner, for its part, addressed the controversy in a note to clients. “Two other Gartner experts in the transportation technology area, as well as the office of the ombuds, [reviewed] the research from beginning to end, to uncover signs of bias or other inappropriate content if it existed,” the note in the report said. “None of these individuals found any evidence of inappropriate content or process missteps in the document.” That this year’s MQ differs little from the 2021 version is unlikely to dampen criticism of the report from project44’s competitors, but analysts leaving to join companies in the sectors they cover is not a new development. In terms of the significance of the report itself, it’s clear that Gartner perceives companies that focus primarily on predictive transportation visibility, analytics and insights derived from the data, and carrier connectivity as being in a stronger position to sell RTTV products than companies with more diversified product sets that happen to also sell visibility. While project44 and FourKites were the only two vendors in the “leaders” quadrant, France-based Shippeo, with a similar and sole focus on visibility, was the next-highest rated provider and placed in the “challengers” quadrant. Overhaul, which focuses on providing visibility as a means for shippers to mitigate supply chain risk, saw its position improve the most from 2021 and 2022 within the challengers quadrant. From a geographic perspective, the report cautioned that most providers outside of project44 and FourKites are overly dependent on customers and carrier connectivity within one region. One issue for companies trying to sell visibility within broader transportation or supply chain management product sets is that it can be difficult to justify the cost of continuing product enhancements and sales and marketing efforts to support those improvements, for what amounts to an ancillary offering. That was made clear to JOC.com this week by a provider in the global trade management space, who asked not to be identified, that is seeing demand from potential customers for an integrated transportation visibility solution. The cost to build it internally might overwhelm what the company could get for a non-core part of its offering, but the absence of such a tool is glaring when compared with other platforms that have it. Another option is using an existing visibility tool or tools in a white-labeled arrangement, but matching up the data schema between those tools and the company’s core GTM product is not as easy as it may seem, the provider said. The report did not include a cadre of niche, internationally focused visibility data providers, such as Vizion, Terminal49, Portcast, and OpenTrack. Those vendors, most of whom have received venture funding, are likely too focused on non-trucking modes or lack the required revenue to be considered for the report. title: Turning supply chain chaos into profitable business
content: LAKE BUENA VISTA, Fla. —Manufacturers have generally weathered the past two years of disruption and now are shifting into future-proofing their businesses, incorporating better visibility and supply chain control. That is one of the takeaways from Fictiv’s seventh annual State of Manufacturing report. Released Monday at the Gartner Supply Chain Sumposium/XPO at Walt Disney World’s Dolphin Resort, the report found a majority (59%) of companies said improving supply chain visibility is their top priority. Nearly two-thirds of respondents (65%) also are looking to increase onshoring to protect against future global supply chain shocks. “What stood out to me in this year’s report was the progress that has been made over the last three years,” said Dave Evans, Fictiv CEO and co-founder. “2020 was about seeing the problems, 2021 was about finding the solutions, and now in 2022, we see companies are making progress towards a future-proofed industry. Leaders are demanding major changes from the ground up in order to gain much-needed control and predictability. Fictiv was founded due to the very issues companies are still facing today, and I’m excited to see momentum toward technology-powered transformation.” In an interview with FreightWaves, Evans said the 10-year-old company saw tremendous growth in the past few years as manufacturers looked for flexibility to the global supply chain disruptions. Fictiv matches firms with manufacturers that have capacity to handle custom and on-demand jobs. Evans pointed to the recent shutdown of Shenzen, China, due to a COVID case spike. “In our model, we had 249 [manufacturing] orders in flight that were affected,” Evans said. “In hours, we were able to shift all of those orders [to other locations].” It is that kind of flexibility that Fictiv thrives on, although the company started as a conduit between businesses building new products and those with manufacturing capacity to handle the limited runs. That remains a primary focus of the business today, but the past few years have opened eyes among supply chain leaders about the need to be more agile, Evans said. “We’ve taken a road map that might have taken five years and been doing it in 18 months,” Evans noted, saying that employee headcount has been almost doubling year-over-year, and the company recently closed a new $100 million financing round. “Supply chain has never been as sexy as it is now.” The Fictiv report had several other interesting findings, including that 88% of manufacturers want to streamline production by reducing the number of suppliers, and 93% are looking for technology solutions to increase operational efficiency for new product development. While reducing suppliers might seem counterintuitive to managing disruptions, Evans said many companies simply have too many suppliers. And at a cost of between $40,000 and $60,000 to manage each one, there is money to be saved. “I don’t think you can meet a supply chain officer that thinks they have the right number of vendors,” he said. The report surveyed 234 senior decision-makers in supply chain, engineering, research and development, and technology or business leadership roles at companies that produce medical devices, robotics, automotive, aerospace or consumer electronics. Evans said over the past three years of the report, there was a definite trend of leaders recognizing there is a supply chain problem in 2020, shifting into solution mode in 2021, and finally transitioning into executive mode this year. “That road map would have taken a decade [to accomplish],” he said. Among the top themes identified is the increased use of digital manufacturing technology and analytics and on-demand manufacturing platforms. Over 90% of companies are now using or implementing digital manufacturing tech, and 61% are using supply chain analytics, while 58% have adopted on-demand manufacturing platforms. Leaders said they are facing fewer barriers to innovation overall, but 97% are concerned about security in a more digitized environment. The report also found that 73% of manufacturing leaders view outsourcing positively and 48% increased outsourcing to deal with the effects of the pandemic. Also, customer demand continued to shift, with more emphasis on sustainability, quality and advanced features among the top asks. However, while increased agility (49% of respondents) and more efficient team coordination (48%) were cited as ways manufacturers are responding to this, 75% said engineering and supply chain teams need to collaborate more. Evans also pointed to security and productivity as big concerns among supply chain leaders. More companies are focused on improving productivity, which reached a decadeslong low in Q1, Evans said. Fictiv is unique in that its solutions are product-agnostic, but the companies must be willing to change. “If you are fine with the status quo, it’s probably not a good fit,” Evans said. “But if you are looking for agility [Fictiv can help].” He noted that Fictiv has helped companies of all sizes, from a 20-person robotics company that it helped save $600,000, to Honeywell, where Fictiv worked to address an issue in its $6 billion aerospace division. title: Gartner expert: Supply chains can thrive even amid disruption
content: LAKE BUENA VISTA, Fla. Relationships. Trust. Control. And visibility. These are the hallmarks of a strategy to managing and surviving supply chain risk, said Brian Whitlock, senior director analyst at Gartner. Speaking at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium/XPO 2022 on Monday at Walt Disney World’s Dolphin Resort in Lake Buena Vista, Florida, Whitlock cited those four items as the call to action during his presentation, titled Logistics Risk and Disruption: Is it in the Past or Forever Part of the Future. Whitlock ran through some survey results from recent Gartner surveys, including that 92% of businesses were impacted by COVID, weather, fuel costs, supply or labor shortages, or some other disruption. “What surprised me was how low these numbers were,” he said. “I can’t think of a single company that wasn’t impacted.” Whitlock said it seems like disruptions just keep “compounding on top of each other,” and businesses maybe facing disruptions for a while still. He broke down the three key challenges facing businesses today: building better relationships, control, visibility. Relationships are important, Whitlock said, pointing to a Gartner survey that found 57% of companies were not considered a shipper of choice. “Companies in this group struggled to get capacity,” he said, pointing to a survey where the three top answers on how to improve “all centered around relationships.” Whitlock cautioned against building only local relationships, saying that doing so could hamper operations if a disruption occurs only on the local level. Control showed up in the surveys as 70% of companies said they wanted to bring some outsourcing back in house. Often, this was around managed transportation, warehousing and fulfillment, and freight and payment solutions. One company that Whitlock said successfully did this was Ashley Furniture, which in 2021 acquired trucking company Wilson Logistics, expanded its North American footprint to pull some overseas manufacturing back to the U.S., and when it had to source goods from overseas, charted vessels to smaller West Coast ports, avoiding some of the backlog that occurred at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Visibility was also a key challenge for companies in the surveys, with 70% saying it was their number-one area of improvement. Whitlock said improved visibility will improve costs through better inventory control and labor management. “Visibility is a journey and takes time to develop,” he said. Ultimately, to overcome the challenges and achieve success, Whitlock said companies should: Whitlock pointed to Dell Technologies as a company that embodies some of what he talked about, noting that Dell leveraged this playbook and in 2021 had record revenues and record profits “in large part due to its supply chain execution.” Click for more articles by Brian Straight. title: Performance Team opening cold storage facility in New Jersey
content: Maersk North America announced Monday its Performance Team will open a nearly 168,000-square-foot cold storage facility in Dayton, New Jersey, in October to serve imports and exports of such commodities as fish, poultry, beef, pork, fruits and vegetables. “We’re adding more cold chain capacity to serve the New York/New Jersey metropolitan-area demand. This intergrates with Maersk’s ocean services and their first port of call in Elizabeth, New Jersey, and the consumption patterns generated by the 20 million consumers who live within the metropolitan area,” Jason Walker, executive vice president of operations for Performance Team – A Maersk Company, said in the announcement. Maersk said it can provide end-to-end supply chain solutions with its ships calling its APM Terminals Elizabeth, followed by clearance through Maersk Customs Services and finally storage, fulfillment distribution and inland transportation through Performance Team, which A.P. Moller – Maersk (OCTUS: AMKBY) acquired in April 2020 in a $545 million acquisition. “Cold chain business in the New York/New Jersey metropolitan area continues strong and our plans are to expand supply chain capacity in this market to serve the growth aspirations of our exporters and importers with our integrated model,” said Diogo Lobo, regional head of cold chain for Maersk North America. The Dayton site was chosen because of its close proximity to the Elizabeth container port, Maersk said. It’s also about a one-hour drive from the Port of Philadelphia and two and a half hours from Baltimore and Delaware. Maersk said the facility will encompass 167,812 square feet, with 13,000 rack positions, 30 dock doors, a dry sprinkler system, refrigerated dock, trailer plug-ins, in-house clearance, refrigerated and frozen storage, 24-hour monitoring, and a backup generator. U.S. Department of Agriculture import and export services, repacking, reboxing, labeling, and co-packing also will be available. Performance Team currently operates more than 60 distribution and fulfillment centers in North America. Maersk added to its North American first-, middle- and last-mile capabilities with its February acquisition of Pilot Freight Services for $1.8 billion. In March, Maersk announced Performance Team would build a 283,000-square-foot cold storage facility in Baytown, Texas, about 15 minutes from Port Houston. The facility, which will have access to both BNSF and Union Pacific rail lines, is expected to open in August. As part of its transformation from a pure ocean carrier to an end-to-end logistics company, Maersk also has looked to the sky. In November, it agreed to pay $644 million to acquire German freight forwarder Senator International, which primarily manages airfreight transportation for cargo owners. title: Monster leans on US sourcing to lower freight costs
content: Aluminum constraints last year had pushed Monster to import more from cans from abroad. However, relying on more imports brought other challenges: port congestion, a lack of shipping containers, and “significant increases in domestic and international freight costs,” Sacks said in August. Monster is now focused on positioning production closer to customers, adding suppliers and rebuilding inventories within the U.S. Sacks said last month adding the two suppliers, which are now operational, should help Monster decrease its reliance on imported aluminum cans. Still, rising aluminum prices continue to present headwinds for the company. Monster saw a “dramatic increase in aluminum prices,” with costs soaring 65% YoY in Q1, President Hilton Schlosberg said. Although Monster has added more suppliers and co-packing capacity in the U.S., the company is still relying on imports to meet demand. The company estimates $46 million in costs were the result of operating inefficiencies “including the importation of aluminum cans,” Sacks said. Beverage can makers are facing similar pressures and are looking to up production in the United States as a way to lower costs. Ball Corporation, which has also imported more aluminum to meet demand, is investing in new ways to increase production in the U.S. The company expects to announce new investments in 2022 “to support domestic U.S. production of aluminum can sheet to further enable long-term growth,” President and CEO Dan Fisher said in the company’s Q1 earnings call. “We’re starting to see investment in the aluminum supply chain in North America,” said CFO Scott Morrison. “So I think that’s encouraging.”

title: FMC needs to expand to increase monitoring, meet OSRA mandates
content: Even before the new funding request, the FMC, which is authorized for 128 employees currently, had been struggling to find new hires. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. US maritime regulators are seeking additional funding to handle increased monitoring of the container shipping industry amid persistent disruption, and they may need even more money depending on the scale of the mandate within pending shipping reform legislation. The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is asking Congress for a 5.2 percent increase in its fiscal year 2023 budget, to $34.7 million, primarily to expand the agency’s workforce from 115 to 150, with the majority of new hires serving in enforcement and customer service roles. The Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA) of 2022, now in reconciliation between the House and Senate before being sent to President Joe Biden for his signature, promises to expand the agency’s authority further, requiring more people and resources. “This investment is needed. Demand for commission services is not dissipating,” FMC Commissioner Dan Maffei said at an April 27 hearing. He added that the agency has had to prioritize its investigations and that the FMC could handle more if it had additional resources. The OSRA bill includes language that would fund the FMC with $4 million more than the agency requested in fiscal 2023, $43.7 million for fiscal year 2024, and $49.2 million for fiscal year 2025. The federal fiscal year begins Oct. 1. Even before the new funding request, the FMC, which is authorized for 128 employees currently, had been struggling to find new hires, according to Commissioner Carl Bentzel. Despite adding substantial staff over the last couple of years, attrition from an aging work force and hiring and training new hires with the desired maritime expertise has kept the commission tally hovering at too low a number that it’s set the FMC behind on calls. “We’re really looking for personnel, but there are not a lot of experts in [the] maritime shipping world pounding down our doors,” Bentzel told JOC.com in an interview Friday. The last two years brought several million dollars in new funding to the FMC’s budget — thanks in large part to the support of President Biden — to increase salaries, and the next three years could see a potential extra $5 million to $6 million annually through the OSRA to expand the workforce. An increased budget would allow the FMC to hire more investigative and enforcement personnel to keep an eye on ocean carriers, alliances, and fees and surcharges. A larger staff would also help the FMC provide ongoing guidance to shippers bringing complaints to the commission and allow it to review —and potentially investigate — more of the hundreds of correspondences the agency has received during the COVID-19 pandemic. Still, Maffei said the biggest challenge for the industry is not regulating ocean carrier behavior, but a need to expand US ports, inland infrastructure, equipment, and labor supply to keep up with cargo demand. “The availability of intermodal equipment, warehouse space, intermodal train service, trucking — and enough workers in each of those sectors — remain challenges to getting more cargo off our ports and to destination with more certainty and reliability,” he said during the hearing. title: Maersk picks NJ for fourth cold-storage warehouse
content: Performance Team, which has 9 million square feet of distribution, also plans to open another cold-storage warehouse in Houston this year. Photo credit: Performance Team. Maersk’s North American warehousing subsidiary plans to open its fourth US cold-storage facility in New Jersey, in a bid to handle more of the refrigerated (reefer) goods going through the Port of New York and New Jersey. Performance Team, which operates over 9 million square feet of distribution space, will open a new 167,812-square-foot facility in Dayton, New Jersey, by October 2022, the company said in a statement Monday. The site, located about 30 miles from the Port of New York and New Jersey, was chosen for its proximity to the port’s marine terminals. Maersk and its north-south carrier subsidiaries, Sealand and Hamburg Süd, both of which specialize in reefer trade, call New York–New Jersey first on many of their US East Coast services The warehouse will have a dedicated truck and chassis fleet to bring reefer containers to the facility for inland distribution. “Cold chain business in the New York–New Jersey metropolitan area continues strong, and our plans are to expand supply chain capacity in this market to serve the growth aspirations of our exporters and importers with our integrated model,” Diogo Lobo, regional head of cold-chain for Maersk, said in the statement. New Jersey has 5.7 million square feet of refrigerated warehousing, according to industrial real estate firm CBRE, making it the 10th largest US cold-storage market. Performance Team said the warehouse will handle commodities such as fish, poultry, beef, pork, and fresh fruits and vegetables. Also accessible from the ports of Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Delaware, the Dayton site is Performance Team’s fourth cold-storage warehouse. It's already opened cold-storage warehouses in Charleston, South Carolina, and Wilmington, North Carolina. Another warehouse near the Port of Houston is expected to be open by August. Maersk acquired Performance Team for $545 million in January 2020 as part of the ocean carrier’s broader effort to become an end-to-end integrated logistics services provider. title: Elephant in the room: Aim to optimize, not cut, logistics costs
content: LAKE BUENA VISTA, Fla. — Ocean rates are up. Trucking rates are high. Airfreight rates are up. And the global supply chain is in crisis. So why does Greg Aimi believe the answer is to eat an elephant? The Gartner vice president of research and logistics technologies hosted a discussion on Tuesday at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium/XPO 2022 conference at Walt Disney World’s Dolphin Resort, aptly titled, “If you want to cost-optimize logistics, learn how to eat an elephant.” His point was that many organizations approach cost optimization through cost cutting, but because logistics is so big — like an elephant — that is not the right approach. “Cost cutting things are different than what you do in cost optimization,” he said, noting that companies often look to cut line items or limit spending, which ultimately hurts the overall profitability of the logistics operation. Aimi laid out a strategy to achieve cost optimization that will set up an organization for the long haul. It starts by not cutting costs in a way that hamper logistics, but rather looking to find ways to invest in areas “to set you up for the future.” An example of this would be looking at workflow automation technologies, he said. A majority of companies — 52% in a recent Gartner survey — reduced their logistics costs by increasing their operational efficiency, not cutting. Secondly, firms should implement a plan. This can be short term (three to nine months), medium term (nine to 18 months) or long term (18-plus months) and in many cases involves all three steps. In the short term, the business should work to operate better, whereas a reconfiguration of the business should be conducted over the medium term. Finally, the long term should be focused on transformation. Companies seeking to operate more efficiently can look at budget items, examine their freight and payment operations, tighten lead times and shorten delivery windows, and improve collaboration on order quantities. Once the medium-term plan goes into effect, the business should be focused on organizational change, operational alignment and tightening of logistics polices while forming partnerships with 3PLs and carriers to remove waste from the operation. Over the long term, Aimi continued, businesses should be investing in logistics-specific systems and digital technologies such as robotics that will reduce labor and improve service. Also, now is the time to look at conducting a “cost-to-service” analysis. “[You] don’t want to overserve where the cost analysis is [not positive],” he said. “Good logistics is the ability to service on a consistent basis,” Aimi continued. “Great logistics is the ability to do so while optimizing cost.” Aimi added that companies should not discount upstream changes. Operations in the sales and order departments, for instance, can have an impact on logistics costs. Logistics, Aimi said, is so big that it always appears to be the elephant in the room. “The way to eat the elephant is to break it up into pieces.” Click for more articles by Brian Straight. title: FMC signaling measured approach ahead of OSRA
content: Using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, a measure of market concentration, the FMC’s Bureau of Trade Analysis found the Asia-US trade to be competitive, according to the Fact Finding 29 report. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The findings of a Federal Maritime Commissioner’s investigation into how the pandemic has impacted container shipping suggest a measured approach moving forward, finding no collusion among carriers but recommending greater monitoring of their activities. A sharper mandate and moderately expanded powers likely to emerge from legislation this year amid President Joe Biden’s rhetoric against carriers do not look as though they will shake the FMC. Rather, the independent agency is exercising more of its power ahead of the first US shipping reform in two decades — although not with the speed to please all. The results of the investigation by Federal Maritime Commissioner Rebecca Dye, released May 31, dismiss the idea that container lines manipulated the market to send spot rates soaring to historic highs, concluding — as many in the industry inherently know — that unprecedented demand outstripped capacity. The cost of shipping a 40-foot container from Shanghai to Los Angeles is up nearly 50 percent from a year ago at $8,704, according to Drewry, well above pre-pandemic levels below $2,000. Using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, a measure of market concentration, the FMC’s Bureau of Trade Analysis found the Asia–US trade to be competitive, according to the Fact Finding 29 report. The index measures market concentration through the lens of pre- and post-mergers and acquisitions. That is key given the number of major carriers on the trans-Pacific and trans-Atlantic trades has shrunk from 20 in 2015 to 11 now. Dye’s report found that carriers blanked sailings due to port congestion, not to drive up rates, a sharp retort to politicians and members of the shipping public who accused ocean carriers of engaging in anticompetitive behavior. And while the alliances as highly integrated vessel-sharing agreements control the majority of the trade, the report did not note any violations, in spite of months of allegations. Carriers outside the three major alliances have a larger slice of the market, according to the report, which ended a two-year investigation. During the worst of the pandemic in the second quarter of 2020, the share of non-alliance carriers in the trans-Pacific market calling the US West Coast was just 12 percent; now it’s approximately 29 percent, according to maritime analyst and JOC analyst Lars Jensen. In terms of East Coast routings, non-alliance carriers saw their shares swing from zero to 15 percent in the same period. The FMC “to date, observed no indication that the current prices for liner shipping are a result of collusion or illegal conduct on the part of the major ocean carriers,” according to Dye’s report. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating Maersk and one other carrier, as tied to a global probe by competition authorities into suspected anticompetitive behavior and collusion with global supply chains. The DOJ in 2019 ended a prior multiyear investigation of carriers without having brought charges, according to carriers including Maersk. A week prior to the release of Fact Finding 29 at a shipper summit, FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said that despite dozens of complaints about higher spot rates, those complaining can’t or are unwilling to provide enough evidence. In two of the three FMC investigations into improper assessment of detention and demurrage fees, two carriers paid major civil penalties in separate cases. The results of agency’s Bureau of Enforcement investigation into the third carrier have not been disclosed yet. “We’ve gotten so many complaints of shipping lines breaking their contracts,” Maffei said at the National Industrial Transportation League’s virtual conference May 23. “When we do look into them, unfortunately we find that most of the time the carrier, while they may have violated the spirit of the contract, the actual letter of the contract somehow gets them out of it.” Congress could change that by further expanding FMC’s power, even going as far as to charge the FMC with setting rates. But the Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA), which is expected to be passed by Congress and head to Biden’s desk in coming weeks, won’t likely go that far. “We can also reduce the cost of everyday goods by fixing broken supply chains, improving infrastructure, and cracking down on the exorbitant fees that foreign ocean freight companies charge to move products,” Biden wrote in a May 30 Wall Street Journal op-ed titled, “My Plan for Fighting Inflation.” Based on both House and Senate versions, the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 at the very least will grant the FMC more power over ocean carrier detention and demurrage billing practices and export services. Perhaps the version of the OSRA being hashed out in conference by Senate and House leaders, will be more dramatic than anyone expected. Or Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., may be exaggerating the impact of the legislation. “The shipping container market is being manipulated and American business owners know it,” Klobuchar, referring to OSRA 2022, tweeted June 1. “While multinational companies make billions more in profit, our exporters are hurting.” Barring a dramatic expansion of FMC’s purview, the agency will likely continue to seek to clarify existing rules and expand its monitoring. Starting May 5, the FMC began requiring alliances and each member company to show more pricing and capacity information. “Additional agreement changes may be required by the Commission to alleviate competition concerns as warranted,” according to Dye’s report. That could include making it easier for the agency to challenge vessel-sharing agreements and give the agreements an expiry date, as they currently don’t have a shelf life. The Fact Finding 29 report proposes rulemaking to clarify and provide consistency on acceptable practices tied to empty container returns, earliest return dates, and carrier and merchant haulage. The FMC should also investigate how container lines, ports, and marine terminals levy charges through tariffs, the report recommended. The five-member commission would have to approve the recommendations in order to pursue them. More activist commissioners than Dye may want to take a more aggressive approach. FMC Commissioner Carl Bentzel wants the agency to provide partial oversight of rail demurrage, for example. Ultimately, though, these are measured moves aimed at providing more structure to commercial exchanges without stepping directly into them. If Congress expects more, it will likely need another shipping act. Contact Mark Szakonyi at mark.szakonyi@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @MarkSzakonyi. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Sustainable packaging goals challenged by supply chain realities
content: In the past two years, several CPGs have announced deadlines to slash their use of virgin plastic in packaging and shift toward more earth-friendly options over the next few decades, including Keurig Dr Pepper, PepsiCo and Mondelēz. Recycled plastic and paper have proven to be two of the more popular alternatives. But as price and supply volatility continue to impact the packaging industry, one question keeps emerging: Is there a clear pathway in the short term to hitting these goals, or are they just pipe dreams? A mix of factors threaten to complicate CPGs’ timelines, including the pandemic’s scrambling of consumer buying behavior and material supply chains, the existing recycling framework in the U.S., as well as recent developments such as the war in Ukraine. This is even as pressure continues to mount for the industry to take accountability over the pollution caused by food and beverage packaging. “There have been a lot of commitments in terms of using recycled content and packaging, and the goals that were established were set without really a fundamental base of the means to do that,” said Robin Waters, director of plastics planning and analysis, IHS Markit, in an interview with Food Dive late last year. To understand why meeting these commitments may prove difficult, it helps to examine the price and supply swings that have rippled across virgin and reclaimed plastic resin over the past two years. The story begins with virgin plastic, resins that are newly created from oil or, as is mostly the case in North America, natural gas. Food manufacturers are under pressure to reduce their use of virgin plastic in packaging, and for good reason. A 2018 study cited by the Association of Plastic Recyclers found recycled plastic resin uses anywhere from 79% to 88% less energy to produce as virgin resin, depending on the type. At different points over the past two years, virgin plastic resin has been considerably more or less expensive than reclaimed plastic as pandemic forces stressed their respective supply chains. And with each shift in the price trend, the timeline to hit goals for cutting virgin plastic also changes. “There have been a lot of commitments in terms of using recycled content and packaging, and the goals that were established were set without really a fundamental base of the means to do that.” Director of plastics planning and analysis, IHS Markit As the pandemic swelled in early 2020, supplies of virgin plastics such as polypropylene — a stiff, recyclable plastic used in packaging such as yogurt containers — shifted to medical purposes like face masks and protective gear. “And so, the factories that were producing these chemicals, polymers, shifted capacity from one type to another, also creating shortages, which also increased the prices,” Richard Freundlich told Fold Dive, a senior analyst of plastics supply chains with RaboResearch, who has retired since the interview. The Gulf Coast also saw brutal weather events, including Winter Storm Uri and Hurricanes Ida and Nicholas in 2021, that knocked out power and throttled the natural gas industry as well as chemical plants in Texas. The chaos had ripple effects further downstream into plastic packaging manufacturing. “Suddenly we have shortages, and you just can’t substitute material so easily in the packaging field because of the food law regulation,” Freundlich said, referring to FDA regulations that restrict which substances can come into contact with food. Swapping out one chemical additive in plastic packaging requires a qualification from the FDA — a process that takes about a year, he noted. The infrastructure outages led to packaging plant shutdowns and plastic shortages. Virgin plastic resins saw a historic price increase during the fallout. Meanwhile, as the cost of virgin resins rose, so naturally did the cost of food packaging, Freundlich noted. To get ahead of these costs, CPG companies began reducing package sizes. This had a supply impact, requiring packaging manufacturers to retool. Reclaimed plastic has faced its own supply stressors. For a time, labor shortages during the pandemic led to packaging plant shutdowns and disrupted recycling operations that fed the market. “When you look at all these plastics when they are reclaimed, they are done historically in the United States by mechanical sorting, and that takes cheap labor,” Freundlich said. “And those are the first guys that quit their jobs [during the pandemic].” More importantly, it also affected the collection of materials for recycling. The result was material shortages and, of course, price increases. “Know all these companies that you read about — ‘We’re going to use 25%, up to 50% of reclaimed plastic in our packages,’ right? That became a pipe dream,” said Freundlich. “Not only because of the sourcing problems, but the price of making reclaimed plastic was significantly higher than the virgin material itself, sometimes twice as expensive. So the promises that were made, will never be met.” While recycled plastics have since become more price competitive recently as virgin plastic faces higher input costs in the wake of the Ukraine war, the lingering supply and demand effects of the pandemic will continue to play out and complicate CPGs’ transition to more sustainable materials. Demand for rPET has also outpaced supply as recycling rates lag. According to the National Association for PET Container Resources, end-use consumption of rPET rose 10% in the U.S. and Canada in 2020, while collection fell about 2.3% in the United States, resulting in a recycling rate of 26.6%. Coca-Cola, which announced in February it would begin using 100% rPET for its bottles, has been working with local governments on setting recycling policy to ensure a supply of quality rPET, spokesperson Bailey Rogers told Food Dive. Structural issues in the plastics recycling industry also are complicating the shift away from virgin plastics. Most plastic in the U.S. is recycled mechanically, through processes that include grinding, washing, separating, drying, re-granulating and compounding. “The ability to supply enough mechanically recycled plastics that can be used to displace virgin plastics is limited for a number of reasons,” said Waters with IHS Markit. He said these include limitations on the types of plastics that can easily be mechanically recycled — the process works best on rigid plastics and thick films — and issues with ensuring the traceability of different plastics once they’ve been processed. “And so we’ve seen that the premium for [post-consumer recycled plastics] go up as the commitments have been made,” Waters said. According to Plastics Recycling Update, the national average price of post-consumer PET beverage bottles and jars rose 17% from March to April, for a per-pound price of 39.22 cents. This compares to 12.03 cents one year ago. Bret Biggers, senior economist with the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries, told Food Dive the recycling industry is responding to growing demand by investing in new plants, equipment and automation, specifically at materials recovery facilities (MRF) that process the commodities after collection and supply them to packaging manufacturers. Private equity is providing a financial boost to some players, allowing them to expand and upgrade, a trend he expects to continue in the year ahead. Labor shortages affecting all of manufacturing are expected to ease in the second half of 2022, Biggers noted. However, many of the issues that affected supply last year will persist in the months ahead. “Supply chain disruptions are going to continue. There’s forecasts it won’t be until the second and third quarter before they start easing,” he said. ”… Within America, the transportation costs are going up and wages. ... That means that recyclers have to contend with a lot of rising costs.” The alternatives to plastic have also seen their own share of price volatility. Different types of paper, which has proven a popular option for CPGs ranging from Bumble Bee with its paperboard tuna can wrappers to Diageo and its paper whisky bottles, has also faced price increases, although at a more modest degree compared to other materials. “Paper packaging prices have gone up about 26% to 44% in the past two years, depending on what kind of grades you’re looking at,” said Xinnan Li, an analyst for food and agribusiness with RaboResearch told Food Dive. “But that’s really driven by a higher consumer demand. Whether it’s on the retail side, consumers just buying more products on the market shelf, or on the e-commerce side, a lot more products have to be packaged in corrugated boxes.” The North American paper market is also fairly consolidated around a handful of major manufacturers, who have a lot of pricing power, Li said. Finally, paper packaging has been wrestling with the same labor issues as other industries, and so both virgin and reclaimed paper manufacturers have passed along the higher associated costs. At the beginning of the pandemic, some MRFs closed, sending demand and prices skyward for old corrugated container pulp (OCC). A jump in demand from online purchases early in the pandemic also was a major factor. Li said the OCC price has jumped from about $30 a ton to now $120. “So that’s a huge increase that … the industry is going to digest somehow,” she said. Prices for wood pulp, the basis of virgin corrugated board, has seen about a 50% price increase, “purely driven by demand for wood for pulp.” Although some of the packaging material price rallies had begun to settle toward the end of 2021, the Ukraine conflict has introduced a new element of uncertainty. While Ukraine is not a major provider of chemicals — with about 3% to 5% of the market, Freundlich said — it does rattle the balance of supply feeding the plastics industry. Meanwhile, with some European countries boycotting Russian natural gas, the U.S. has stepped in to supply liquified natural gas. That diverted supply will come at the expense of industries such as plastic manufacturing. “When you add all this together, it’s inflation. It will be continued inflation. And even before the Ukraine situation, we would see moderate price increases in packaging resins for the next five to 10 years because of natural gas,” Freundlich said. Freundlich said the quickly shifting ground makes providing a forecast on virgin plastics pricing difficult. “Plants have been canceled. Pipelines have been canceled,” he said. “We don’t know what the effect is and how the import-export relationships will be altered. This all could have major effects on price. So ‘hold on tight’ is what I’m saying. Yes, it’s not going down. It’s going to be an inflationary year.” Perhaps the biggest factor in materials costs will be energy. The Ukraine conflict pushed the price of global benchmark Brent crude oil to $134 per barrel this past March — its highest point since 2008 — and U.S. natural gas prices to their highest level in 13 years. Brent crude prices have since settled to around $110 per barrel, although demand is expected to remain elevated. “When you add all this together, it’s inflation. It will be continued inflation. And even before the Ukraine situation, we would see moderate price increases in packaging resins for the next five to 10 years because of natural gas.” Retired senior analyst, plastics supply chains, RaboResearch For recycled plastics, this provides an opening. At the Plastics Recycling Conference this past March, analysts with IHS Markit noted the runup in oil prices could pressure virgin resin prices and make recycled resins more competitive, Waste Dive reported. Beyond being a key material in plastics, oil and natural gas also power most of global manufacturing. This has implications for the economics of different packaging types. “Energy costs — if you look at glass — whoa. Aluminum — yikes. I mean, these are all very, very energy-intensive,” Freundlich said of other virgin packaging alternatives to plastic. “It’s a scary situation. But the good news is there’s lots of new capacity coming online and that can counteract some of the costs.” Paper prices are also being pressured by the war. “Before we were forecasting double-digit growth even before the Russia-Ukraine [conflict],” Li said. Because paper processing is energy-intensive, the war will only pressure prices in the short term. Longer term, Li said the outlook for paper prices is much better, with several new corrugated container board plants due to come online and capacity expansions that should add to supply. This — combined with the more modest price swings for paper — could give the material an advantage as more manufacturers shift their packaging. “With where the traditional plastic prices are, that could be even more incentive for companies to look into the alternative — more sustainable materials. Because traditionally, sustainable materials are more expensive,” Li said. Meanwhile, another buzzword is bubbling up that will affect both the food and packaging industries in the years to come. “Over the last three, four years, everybody, including every packaging person, was stuck up on the word ‘sustainability,’” Freundlich said. “This year and the following couple years, that word will be changed to ‘decarbonization.’” To build on the Paris climate accord, the United Nations is challenging every country, city, company and financial institution to strive for carbon neutrality by 2050. Food companies including Nestlé, Mars and Unilever have already set targets for net zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. Packaging is one path to meeting those goals. “There’s not one company that doesn’t have a team very significantly considering what they can do,” Freundlich said. “It’s going to have a great impact on inflation and unfortunately cost as well.”

title: Biden to ocean carriers: ‘The rip-off is over’
content: Making the case for legislation to hold carriers more responsible for shipping costs and service standards, President Joe Biden on Friday laid much of the blame for record-setting inflation data released earlier in the day on the decks of the world’s largest ocean carriers. “Every once in a while something you learn makes you viscerally angry,” Biden said, speaking at the Port of Los Angeles. “That’s why I’ve called on Congress to crack down on foreign-owned shipping companies that have raised their prices while raking in just last year $190 billion in profit, a sevenfold increase in one year.” He repeated assertions in a video released by the White House on Thursday that nine major ocean shipping companies in the trans-Pacific trade have raised rates by as much as 1,000%, implying that lack of competition is the root of the problem. In a report issued earlier this month, however, the Federal Maritime Commission found no evidence of collusion among the major carriers. Biden is presumably referring to alliance members Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM, Cosco, Evergreen, HMM, Hapag-Lloyd, ONE, and Yang Ming (which leaves out Zim, which is also a major player in the trans-Pacific trade). According to Sea-Intelligence, the alliances accounted for roughly 80-85% of capacity in the trans-Pacific trade in 2012-2020, but in the first four months of 2022, their share had fallen to 64%. Several of the companies contacted by FreightWaves were not immediately available to comment. “We have to keep coming together to find common ground and solve problems,” Biden said. “There’s no better place to start than right here at the port and letting those nine foreign [carriers] understand: The rip-off is over.” Congress is expected to take up the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 as early as next week. Biden said he would sign it into law if it passes. The legislation broadens the regulatory powers of the Federal Maritime Commission over container ship carriers while also promoting U.S. exports. “It’s a big deal,” Biden said. “People at home trying to make it paycheck to paycheck are wondering, ‘What in God’s name do nine shipping companies have to do with it?’ Well almost everything you’re doing — to what you’re eating, to what you’re having to drive, to what you need in your home — is related to the supply chain, which comes from abroad.” Biden was introduced by Sal DiCostanzo, a member of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU), which is negotiating a new contract with West Coast marine terminal operators. The industry is watching those talks closely because a protracted delay in reaching an agreement could spark a new level of port disruption if an impasse leads to work slowdowns or stoppages. Automation is widely understood to be the front-and-center issue. “What is really important for management is to explain why [automation] is needed, not just because we feel like we want to do it,” said Tim Lynch, senior director at the law firm Morgan & Lewis and a consultant to the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which is negotiating the contract on behalf of terminal management. Lynch was providing an update on the ILWU-PMA talks at the National Industrial Transportation League’s annual transportation summit on May 26. “It’s got to be a shared, ‘We’re in this together’” message, Lynch said. “We’ve got to grow these facilities, grow the volume. They’re going to reach capacity in 2028 — what happens after that? They stay stagnant. That’s certainly not good for the carriers, the terminal operators, and it surely shouldn’t be good for the longshoremen.” Click for more FreightWaves articles by John Gallagher. Past the hype. Lynch was providing an update on the ILWU-PMA talks at the National Industrial Transportation League’s annual transportation summit on May 26. “It’s got to be a shared, ‘We’re in this together’” message, Lynch said. “We’ve got to grow these facilities, grow the volume. They’re going to reach capacity in 2028 — what happens after that? They stay stagnant. That’s certainly not good for the carriers, the terminal operators, and it surely shouldn’t be good for the longshoremen.” Click for more FreightWaves articles by John Gallagher. Past the hype. title: Cargobase expands to Mexico to ride manufacturing momentum
content: The last year has seen a wave of investment into Latin American logistics technology, including into cross-border freight brokers and forwarders serving the Mexico market. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Transportation procurement and management technology provider Cargobase has opened a new office in Mexico, a signal there is growing demand for coordinating manufacturing activity there with transportation networks into the US. The new office, in Mexico City, expands Singapore-headquartered Cargobase’s North American footprint beyond its New York office. “Prior to the pandemic, we were already seeing companies across industries expand and move their manufacturing activities from the US and Asia to Mexico,” Cargobase CEO Wiebe Helder said in a statement Thursday. “During the pandemic, we noticed that more companies are, as well, setting up logistics operations and control towers in Mexico to serve the entire North American region.” Helder said Cargobase doesn’t want to only serve demand in the region, but actively “drive and participate in it.” “The pool of talent here is amazing and has the energy we as a scale-up need to grow,” he said. The office will also serve growing demand in South America, where Cargobase is seeing adoption in Brazil and Uruguay, Helder said. Founded in 2013, Cargobase provides an international transportation management system, which it launched in September, to shippers. The company originally emerged as a platform for spot procurement freight. It also has freight visibility, invoice audit and payment, and analytics modules. Customers include automotive parts maker Continental, Bosch, and Siemens. Cargobase expects to have a staff of 10 in the Mexico City office by the end of the third quarter. Outside of Singapore and New York, it operates other offices in the Netherlands and India. The new office highlights growing investment in the Latin American logistics technology market, stretching into Mexico as a two-way resource for logistics activity with the US and Canada and as a gateway into Central and South America. “We believe having a local presence in Mexico is key to accomplishing the growth targets that we’ve set for the company,” Helder said in the statement. In the last year, there have been huge funding rounds into cross-border freight platforms and digital freight forwarders, such as Nowports and Nuvocargo. Cross-border truckload marketplace Forager was acquired in January by Texas-based broker Arrive Logistics. Chile-based digital forwarder KLog has also seen growth during the pandemic and is eyeing expansion in Mexico. title: Urban Outfitters trims low-profit SKUs to boost margins
content: Cancelations of low-selling items, particularly in the men’s category, was accompanied by larger — and earlier — orders of the products Urban Outfitters did offer in Q1. The company did not respond to a request by Supply Chain Dive for the percentage or number of SKU cuts. “We’ve lowered some of the style counts and then raised the quantities that we’re ordering, which has driven some very nice increases in [initial markup value] in several cases,” Hayne said during the Q1 call. Plenty of companies have slimmed their product lines, often prioritizing their most profitable or core products, amid supply chain disruptions in the past few years. It’s a pandemic-era playbook used by Hershey, Coca-Cola, Molendez, Bed Bath & Beyond, HanesBrands and more. Lead times four to six weeks longer than before the pandemic led Urban Outfitters to shift from its previous lean supply chain strategy and pull forward orders of holiday and home products last year. The retailer is still relying on that strategy, as it expects heightened freight rates and other supply chain turbulence to continue through Q2. “That’s what we believe is the right thing to do to protect sales,” Conforti said. “And we’re going to continue to do that.” Urban Outfitters’ supply chain woes motivated “a complete review of our business practices with an eye to finding margin builders including logistics efficiencies,” Hayne said in Q4. The company set a 500 basis point initial markup improvement goal after high freight and landing costs tanked the metric by 300 basis points from FY2020 to FY2021. In addition to SKU cuts, the three-year plan includes product distortion, fabric positioning, 3-D product design technology adoption, raising retail prices and relying more on ocean transportation than airfreight. Reaching the initial markup goal will take time, Conforti said during the Q1 call. “These strategies have a longer lead time [and] we’re going to need to see a more steady ground and more normalization in the supply chain inbound freight costs than where we’re at right now,” Conforti said.

title: Biden makes final push for OSRA as House vote nears
content: President Joe Biden’s remarks at the Port of Los Angeles came the same day a group of more than 90 trade associations sent a letter to the leadership of the House and Senate urging final passage of OSRA. Photo credit: Screenshot taken from official White House video feed. President Joe Biden used the backdrop of the Port of Los Angeles Friday to push for final approval of the most significant reform of US shipping law in almost a quarter century. His remarks at the country’s busiest port came as the House of Representatives prepared to vote next week on a final version of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA) of 2022. “One of the key ways to fight inflation is by lowering the cost of moving goods through the supply chain,” Biden said, specifically calling out the major foreign shipping companies transporting goods from Asia to the US West Coast. “The Senate passed legislation and I’m hopeful the House is going to act soon to crack down on these companies like I’ve asked and lower the cost,” Biden said. The president has publicly called out ocean carriers several times in recent months, most notably in his March 1 State of the Union address. “There’s no better place to start than right here at the port, letting those nine foreign shippers understand the rip-off is over,” Biden said Friday. The House, meanwhile, is expected to vote early next week on the unchanged Senate version of OSRA, which the Senate approved in late March. If approved, as expected, the legislation will go to Biden for his signature and become law. OSRA would shift the onus of proving that container storage fees meet shipping law from the shipper to the container line, while strengthening oversight of container lines’ exporting responsibilities, known as common carriage. The Senate bill would require container lines to certify that their detention and demurrage fees comply with US shipping laws. The legislation also calls for the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to create rulemaking to set a standard when carriers could refuse to load exports and to monitor how many exports each container line handles. OSRA would further allow the FMC to self-initiate investigations into container lines’ business practices without having to wait for a formal complaint from the industry. The Senate version, however, does not contain the more restrictive language in the House bill when it comes to carriers handling exports and making equipment available. The vote by the House would come two weeks after FMC Commissioner Rebecca Dye announced the results of a two-year investigation into the impact of the pandemic on container shipping. The FMC found the container shipping market is competitive and that record freight rates are the result not of collusion among carriers, but rather demand overwhelming vessel capacity. The FMC would receive more funding to monitor the industry under OSRA, with the Senate version of the bill authorizing $164 million for agency through fiscal year 2025. Biden’s remarks came the same day a group of more than 90 trade associations sent a letter to the leadership of the House and Senate urging final passage of OSRA. “As US companies continue to face ongoing supply chain disruptions and congestion in addition to rising inflation, it is critical for Congress to address these issues,” the groups wrote. “Final passage of OSRA will help address the longstanding, systemic supply chain and port disruption issues that existed prior to the pandemic as the industry has changed significantly since the last time the Shipping Act was amended over 20 years ago.” Contact Teri Errico Griffis at teri.griffis@ihsmarkit.com. © 2026 S&P Global. title: US ocean shipping reform heads to Biden after House approval
content: The World Shipping Council pledged to work with the FMC to implement OSRA in a way that won’t further disrupt shipping. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. (This story has been updated with comment from the Agriculture Transportation Coalition.) The House of Representatives Monday overwhelmingly approved the most widespread reform to US shipping law in almost a quarter century. While more moderate than the chamber’s original version, the bill will nonetheless significantly overhaul regulation of the container shipping industry once President Joe Biden signs the legislation into law later this week, as he has promised. The Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA) of 2022, passed by a vote of 369-42, shifts the burden of proof on long-contentious detention and demurrage billing practices from shippers and consignees to container lines. The bill will also strengthen the US Federal Maritime Commission’s (FMC's) monitoring of container lines’ responsibility to load exports, otherwise known as their “common carriage” responsibilities. The finalized OSRA 2022 is the version passed by the Senate in late March and is less aggressive than the House’s original legislation, passed overwhelmingly in December, which would have gone so far as to make it illegal for carriers to refuse equipment or service to exporters, while ordering regulators to set service standards for shipping contracts. The Agriculture Transportation Coalition saluted passage of OSRA, but indicated it will push to ensure the federal government utilizes the new tools at its disposal once the bill becomes law. “The Federal Maritime Commission will have to continue to demonstrate its recent and unprecedented will to fully utilize its long held and now expanded authority, as it has done recently in aggressive demurrage and detention enforcement,” the group said in a statement late Monday. AgTC said the new levers provided by OSRA must be used to their full extent because too much is at stake. “There is virtually nothing in US agriculture and forest products grown or produced in this country that cannot be sourced or substituted with products from elsewhere in the world,” it said. “If we cannot deliver affordably and dependably, our foreign customers can, and have proven they will, shift their purchases to those other countries, sometimes permanently.” The National Industrial Transportation League (NITL) also welcomed the passage of the bill, arguing OSRA will give the FMC greater ability to monitor and curb “global ocean carriers’ operating practices which have contributed to high inflation and supply chain disruptions.” NITL was the first shipper group to put forth proposals to Congress on how to reform shipping regulation. The World Shipping Council (WSC), which represents major container lines, pledged to work with the FMC to implement the bill in a way that won’t further disrupt shipping. The group also blasted unspecified federal and Congressional representatives that had grossly mischaracterized the carriers as manipulating the market. “Until the import congestion is remedied, export congestion will persist,” John Butler, president and CEO of the WSC, said in a statement Monday. Biden, with the Port of Los Angeles as a backdrop, on Friday called for the passage of OSRA 2022 and told container lines, who he blames for pushing up inflation via higher prices, that “the rip-off is over.” Still, a two-year investigation by the FMC didn’t find any signs of collusion among carriers, echoing the message of the agency’s chairman. Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. and the sponsor of the original House bill, likewise said in a floor debate preceding the vote that OSRA 2022, “attacks inflation and it will reduce consumer costs, but it’s not going to solve every problem in the supply chain or every problem for US exporters. But it will make a very real difference for American businesses and consumers by lowering the exorbitant ocean shipping costs and prohibiting unfair business practices by foreign-flag ocean carriers.” But OSRA 2022 doesn’t include any language that would rein in the record container rates that have driven historic profits for the industry. Still, OSRA may deter some storage fee billing by requiring carriers to provide more accurate information. The House’s original version would have also directed the FMC to set service level standards within service contracts, something the final version does not. title: Flexport’s mystique meets cold reality of chaotic supply chain
content: One potential route for Flexport would be cross-border e-commerce, a world that future CEO Dave Clark knows well. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. As a journalist covering shipping and logistics, I have followed Ryan Petersen since before he founded Flexport in 2013. Prior to Flexport, Petersen in his 20s created a vigorous competitor to JOC.com sister company PIERS called Import Genius, showing early on his reservoir of ambition, marketing flair, and fluency with both the rhetoric and application of technology. It did not take long for the impression to settle in that Peterson’s new creation, Flexport, was something different than anything that had come before it. When it became apparent that he had found a sweet spot no one even knew existed at the nexus of Silicon Valley and international trade, where trade suddenly became the ultimate “problem” for software engineers to solve, forwarders that had dominated the space for decades suddenly found themselves face to face with an entirely unfamiliar species of competition. But as time went on, that initial shock wore off. The company grew steadily in size and stature, but a realization took hold among competitors that Flexport was not the existential threat it was initially thought to be. The hiring of Amazon operations czar Dave Clark as CEO, a massive recruitment success by any measure, underscored Flexport’s potential, but just as importantly shed light on what it still has yet to achieve nearly a decade since Peterson founded the company. Flexport today is acknowledged as top-tier player in the forwarding space, quite an achievement in a relatively short period of time. But larger forwarders who were initially spooked by the Flexport mystique are now more relaxed about their presence in the market, telling JOC.com they infrequently encounter the company on the competitive field of battle, or that they have won back certain customers initially lost to the San Francisco-based company. Part of the reason for that is a disconnect between its stated aspirations and what it has actually become. No apparent new business concept resembling the “operating system of global trade,” which Peterson pledged to create, has yet to emerge. A realization took hold that forwarding, no matter how technologically adept you are, remains largely a business of resolving so-called exceptions, which occur not just every day, but every hour or every minute, depending on how busy or big you are. The trucker doesn’t show up. You have to plead with the ocean carrier for a container. The terminal gate closed early. And those exceptions, for the most part, are not easily solved, or solvable at all, with technology. Thus, comments made as part of last week’s announcement of Clark joining Flexport in September as co-CEO with Peterson and then becoming sole CEO by March 2023 were at least potentially very revealing as to its progress thus far and potential changes in its strategy going forward. According to a flattering article published in Forbes on June 8, Flexport “still has more than $1 billion of the $2 billion-plus it’s raised to date in the bank.” That shows both the company’s dominance of venture capital investments in the logistics space — it has raised far more VC funding than any other logistics start up by far — but also begs the question of whether the company is encountering limits in its ability to invest that money, although Peterson did note that an early cash flow scare left him conservative on spending. In the Forbes article, Clark acknowledged that Flexport is still years away from achieving its ambitions and may be considering a change in strategy. “If in five years, when you say, ‘What’s the most important company in global supply chain, and in technology across global supply chain?’ if Flexport isn’t the answer, then we messed this up,” he told the magazine. So how would Flexport become “the most important company in global supply chain?” In the ocean space, the landscape is increasingly complex. In a LinkedIn post announcing his new stint at Flexport, Clark said “fast, reliable delivery services … has become clearer over the past two years during the global pandemic.” But with global container ship schedule reliability hovering at a baleful 34 percent, down from 80 percent in December 2019, according to Sea-Intelligence Maritime Analysis, the reality is forwarders — unless they were to go down the road of directly operating ships and terminals — don’t control their own destiny in ocean transportation. Forwarders have no choice but to build relationships with ocean carriers to lock in the vessel capacity that in today’s world is at the heart of forwarders’ credibility with shippers. The need to do that is relatively new for Flexport, which grew up in a pre-pandemic era of abundant ocean capacity and was primarily focused on technology. And even having built carrier relationships, forwarders are still at the whim of the carriers and their newfound market power in terms of being able to offer contract rates and reliable service to shippers. That might change one day; the market is softening headed into the 2022 peak season and a deluge of new capacity will arrive beginning late next year. But for the moment, it’s the carriers who remain in the driver’s seat. Continuing as a trailblazer, Flexport could seek to re-define the industry and go down the asset route, acquiring ships and terminals to gain control over its services, or build up an asset network in the domestic space. But the Forbes piece noted, “Don’t necessarily expect Flexport to build out more of its own assets, the way that Amazon built up capabilities to counter its dependence on FedEx and UPS.” But that doesn’t mean Flexport might not pivot. One potential route would be to grease the wheels of cross-border e-commerce, a world that Clark knows well. It is already playing in that space; Flexport and SF Express, a Chinese express delivery giant, announced a partnership in 2019. And the e-commerce engine Shopify — an Amazon rival — was part of the investor group, together with famed Silicon Valley investor Andreessen Horowitz, that in February committed $935 million to Flexport in a Series E funding round that valued the company at $8 billion. In the Forbes piece, Clark signaled that Flexport may be looking to build out an end-to-end, light-asset model, perhaps leveraging its famed UX up and down the supply chain — a strategy for sure, but a different one. Clark told Forbes he “was intrigued by the opportunity to move Flexport from solving cross-border shipping to a broader solution ‘across the full length of the supply chain.’” Contact Peter Tirschwell at peter.tirschwell@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @petertirschwell. © 2026 S&P Global.
