Prior to Flexport, Petersen in his 20s created a vigorous competitor to JOC.com sister company PIERS called Import Genius, showing early on his reservoir of ambition, marketing flair, and fluency with both the rhetoric and application of technology. It did not take long for the impression to settle in that Peterson’s new creation, Flexport, was something different than anything that had come before it. When it became apparent that he had found a sweet spot no one even knew existed at the nexus of Silicon Valley and international trade, where trade suddenly became the ultimate “problem” for software engineers to solve, forwarders that had dominated the space for decades suddenly found themselves face to face with an entirely unfamiliar species of competition. But as time went on, that initial shock wore off. The company grew steadily in size and stature, but a realization took hold among competitors that Flexport was not the existential threat it was initially thought to be. The hiring of Amazon operations czar Dave Clark as CEO, a massive recruitment success by any measure, underscored Flexport’s potential, but just as importantly shed light on what it still has yet to achieve nearly a decade since Peterson founded the company. Flexport today is acknowledged as top-tier player in the forwarding space, quite an achievement in a relatively short period of time. But larger forwarders who were initially spooked by the Flexport mystique are now more relaxed about their presence in the market, telling JOC.com they infrequently encounter the company on the competitive field of battle, or that they have won back certain customers initially lost to the San Francisco-based company. Part of the reason for that is a disconnect between its stated aspirations and what it has actually become. No apparent new business concept resembling the “operating system of global trade,” which Peterson pledged to create, has yet to emerge. A realization took hold that forwarding, no matter how technologically adept you are, remains largely a business of resolving so-called exceptions, which occur not just every day, but every hour or every minute, depending on how busy or big you are. The trucker doesn’t show up. You have to plead with the ocean carrier for a container. The terminal gate closed early. And those exceptions, for the most part, are not easily solved, or solvable at all, with technology. Thus, comments made as part of last week’s announcement of Clark joining Flexport in September as co-CEO with Peterson and then becoming sole CEO by March 2023 were at least potentially very revealing as to its progress thus far and potential changes in its strategy going forward. According to a flattering article published in Forbes on June 8, Flexport “still has more than $1 billion of the $2 billion-plus it’s raised to date in the bank.” That shows both the company’s dominance of venture capital investments in the logistics space — it has raised far more VC funding than any other logistics start up by far — but also begs the question of whether the company is encountering limits in its ability to invest that money, although Peterson did note that an early cash flow scare left him conservative on spending. In the Forbes article, Clark acknowledged that Flexport is still years away from achieving its ambitions and may be considering a change in strategy. “If in five years, when you say, ‘What’s the most important company in global supply chain, and in technology across global supply chain?’ if Flexport isn’t the answer, then we messed this up,” he told the magazine. So how would Flexport become “the most important company in global supply chain?” In the ocean space, the landscape is increasingly complex. In a LinkedIn post announcing his new stint at Flexport, Clark said “fast, reliable delivery services … has become clearer over the past two years during the global pandemic.” But with global container ship schedule reliability hovering at a baleful 34 percent, down from 80 percent in December 2019, according to Sea-Intelligence Maritime Analysis, the reality is forwarders — unless they were to go down the road of directly operating ships and terminals — don’t control their own destiny in ocean transportation. Forwarders have no choice but to build relationships with ocean carriers to lock in the vessel capacity that in today’s world is at the heart of forwarders’ credibility with shippers. The need to do that is relatively new for Flexport, which grew up in a pre-pandemic era of abundant ocean capacity and was primarily focused on technology. And even having built carrier relationships, forwarders are still at the whim of the carriers and their newfound market power in terms of being able to offer contract rates and reliable service to shippers. That might change one day; the market is softening headed into the 2022 peak season and a deluge of new capacity will arrive beginning late next year. But for the moment, it’s the carriers who remain in the driver’s seat. Continuing as a trailblazer, Flexport could seek to re-define the industry and go down the asset route, acquiring ships and terminals to gain control over its services, or build up an asset network in the domestic space. But the Forbes piece noted, “Don’t necessarily expect Flexport to build out more of its own assets, the way that Amazon built up capabilities to counter its dependence on FedEx and UPS.” But that doesn’t mean Flexport might not pivot. One potential route would be to grease the wheels of cross-border e-commerce, a world that Clark knows well. It is already playing in that space; Flexport and SF Express, a Chinese express delivery giant, announced a partnership in 2019. And the e-commerce engine Shopify — an Amazon rival — was part of the investor group, together with famed Silicon Valley investor Andreessen Horowitz, that in February committed $935 million to Flexport in a Series E funding round that valued the company at $8 billion. In the Forbes piece, Clark signaled that Flexport may be looking to build out an end-to-end, light-asset model, perhaps leveraging its famed UX up and down the supply chain — a strategy for sure, but a different one. Clark told Forbes he “was intrigued by the opportunity to move Flexport from solving cross-border shipping to a broader solution ‘across the full length of the supply chain.’” Contact Peter Tirschwell at peter.tirschwell@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @petertirschwell. © 2026 S&P Global. title: A year after JBS cyberattack, food suppliers remain prime targets for ransomware
content: Food and agriculture businesses remain vigilant one year after JBS USA suffered a ransomware attack in late May 2021 that temporarily shut down its slaughter plants and meat processing in North America and Australia. The U.S. subsidiary of Brazil’s JBS SA, the world’s largest meat supplier, processes about 20% of America’s meat supply. The company paid $11 million in ransom to cybercriminals a week after discovering the incursion. Potential points of entry span a sweeping supply chain, legacy equipment and systems that lack modern security tools. Threat actors are exploiting these weaknesses when companies are most vulnerable. Multiple cyberattacks have hit the industry during the past year, and the FBI recently warned food and agriculture cooperatives could be prime targets during the critical planting and harvest seasons. The agricultural machinery producer AGCO was hit with a ransomware attack on May 5, just 16 days after the FBI warning. Most of the security teams in food and agriculture are still cataloging assets and identifying connected systems with the greatest exposure, Gartner research VP Katell Thielemann told Cybersecurity Dive in an email. A trend is emerging, following targeted attacks during the height of the citrus export season on JBS, agriculture and farming supply coops, machinery producers and South African ports, Thielemann said. “Food and agriculture seems to be on a few peoples’ radars these days in a way we haven’t seen before,” Thielemann said. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) designates food and agriculture as one of the 16 U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, encompassing about 2.1 million farms, 935,000 restaurants and at least 200,000 production and processing facilities. While food and agriculture businesses are aware of the threat posed by ransomware, particularly after a spate of highly publicized and damaging attacks last year, many remain unprepared to counteract the risk. Threat actors initiated ransomware attacks against six grain cooperatives during last fall’s harvest, followed by two attacks earlier this year, potentially disrupting the supply of seeds and fertilizers, according to the FBI. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the global food supply crunch. Food prices have soared almost 30% in the past year, according to the United Nations. Other macroeconomic factors are also testing the industry’s ability to feed people, including grain shortages, climate change, and the highest inflation rates in decades. Operational technology (OT) assets, widespread in the food and agriculture sector, are partly to blame for the security risk. “Much of their machinery runs on legacy OT that was never designed to be connected to the internet,” Grant Geyer, chief product officer at Claroty, said via email. “OT networks predate the internet, and with digital transformation leading organizations to automate parts of their production processes, OT is suddenly being exposed to a whole host of new cyberthreats lurking the web.” Food and agriculture businesses rely on a broad ecosystem that requires extensive information sharing among farmers, transportation companies, processors and distributors. This includes a vast pool of third-party automation vendors that maintain site-to-site access into the OT environment, Geyer said. “With so many potential OT entry points, attackers don’t even need to transit the IT/OT boundary to wreak havoc,” he said. Security teams must consider resiliency of the entire supply chain, including multiple handoffs, while also contending with some outdated systems and equipment that can’t be patched frequently during round-the-clock operations. Commonly exploitable vulnerabilities, such as weak or obsolete user credentials, were the culprit behind many recent attacks. Consolidation and a concentration of companies responsible for the global food supply presents another unique point of risk, according to Thielemann. Food shortages during COVID-19 and the more recent baby formula shortage spotlight the industry’s lackluster resiliency and potentially far-reaching impacts. “A coordinated attack on food and agriculture would lead to empty shelves nationwide in under a week,” Thielemann said. “And you don’t raise chickens or corn at will.”

title: European tech provider targeting US container release bottlenecks
content: Flowfox’s original product helps shipping lines enable street turns, but the company has expanded to import process automation and coordinating container releases from terminals. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Hamburg-based software provider Flowfox is adapting its shipment coordination software from its European home market to the US to leverage opportunities in key North American container gateways. Flowfox sells its product to shipping lines with the intent to help them automate coordination of container releases to their import customers and drop-offs of empty containers, as well as amendments to empty pickup information and re-use of import containers for export loads. Flowfox CEO Patrick Pehmöller told JOC.com this week the company is conducting proofs of concept in the US with three of the largest global container lines and a network of forwarders, including six of the world’s largest third-party logistics providers, such as Kuehne + Nagel. Part of the project is accounting for differences in container gate processes in Europe versus North America. Pehmöller said that while Europe requires a container release number — called a PIN — that’s valid for a limited period of time, no such code is typically required in the US. “That sounds better, but it’s less transparent because only the consignee has the right to get this data unless there is a power of attorney for the forwarder to get this data,” he said. Indeed, as an example, Maersk’s website notes that “release of your container is subject to local customs regulations, charges being paid, and all relevant documents surrendered to the local Maersk office.” “The US container release is a passive process,” Pehmöller said. “In Europe, you have to pull each time. In Europe, the terminal is responsible for customs release, while in the US, it’s the carriers.” Ultimately, Flowfox is aiming to “make it possible to pull [the container] one time and receive always, no matter the region,” Pehmöller said. “We see huge potential to largely automate the import processes with our ocean carrier partners and we are now starting to pilot the Flowfox platform in Europe with major ocean carriers, with the aim to roll out the solution globally,” Markus Johannsen, senior vice president, global ocean freight, at Kuehne + Nagel, said in a statement to JOC.com. Flowfox’s ambition is to automate a number of processes managed by container line import teams and logistics departments, including container repositioning and claims resolution around detention and demurrage assessment. By doing so, it not only makes carrier operations more efficient and improves customer service for its shipper and forwarder clients, it can also increase the carrier’s ability to generate revenue on a per-box basis. More specifically, Flowfox said the top four container lines globally generated an average of $37.98 in operating profit per container between 2010 and 2019. The company believes it can help carriers generate an additional $20 per import box though cost reduction, better equipment utilization, more accurate fee collection, and upselling other services. “There is often a high degree of attention to the part of the process related to selling freight, booking freight, and shipping freight, whereas the import process at times appears to be an afterthought,” said Lars Jensen, CEO of Vespucci Maritime and a member of Flowfox’s advisory board who is also a contributor to JOC.com. “However, as has become extremely visible in the past two years, the import process is also in need of streamlining in order to improve cargo flow and unlock value related to hold-ups in the process.” Forwarders and shippers benefit through enhanced efficiency related to container availability status and the payments required to release a container. Forwarders and shippers can also use the Flowfox platform for free to calculate real-time detention and demurrage costs, provide instructions about container deliver on carrier haulage moves — also known as door moves — and to convey changes to container pickups and drop-offs. Massive profits for liner carriers over the past two years notwithstanding, Pehmöller said carriers are leaving revenue-generating opportunities on the table. “It all leads to unused sales opportunities for carriers, from carrier haulage to customs clearance, visibility or insurance,” he said. As an example, for carrier haulage, the system asks a shipper where and when they want a container, so the carrier can plan resources and availability earlier in the process. “Our focus on container reuse and detention leads naturally to export release,” Pehmöller said. “The depot is not connecting to the ocean carrier in real time, so sometimes an export party goes to pick up a container but it’s not ready or even there. Importers have to ask their carrier, then the carrier literally calls the terminal to determine status and whether it is block-stacked, and then it’s relayed back to the importers.” He said Flowfox wants to make the process less murky through application programming interfaces (APIs) to container terminals, port community systems, shippers, and customs authorities. title: Layoffs signal uncertain times in logistics tech sector
content: Convoy and Stord, two of the most prominent technology names to emerge in the last decade, both raised money in 2022 and laid off employees in the past month. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Broad concern in the early-stage software sector about the direction of the US economy has bled into the world of logistics technology in recent weeks as companies brace for a market with potentially less money to invest in solutions. Over the past few weeks, so-called unicorns Convoy and Stord both confirmed employee layoffs at the high single-digit percent level. The workforce reductions were notable because both Seattle-based Convoy and Atlanta-based Stord had raised significant capital within the last two months, ostensibly to gird themselves against a downturn. A May 26 message to JOC.com from a supply chain investor who asked not to be named looks prescient in retrospect: “No public layoffs yet, but they're definitely happening.” A week later, Business Insider reported Stord laying off 59 employees, about 8 percent of its workforce. A week after that, Convoy confirmed it was laying off 7 percent of its staff, approximately 90 employees. “We have made a number of organizational and other operating expense-related changes to ensure we are in the strongest financial position possible ahead of the potential for worsening economic conditions,” a Convoy spokesman told JOC.com. “This decision was not easy, nor taken lightly. With our recent fundraise behind us and the continued intrinsic strength of our business, we look forward to continuing to improve the freight industry...whatever market conditions we encounter along the way.” Delhi-based last mile visibility provider FarEye also reduced its headcount last week by around 7 percent, a company spokeswoman told JOC.com. Another red flag emerged over the past week, with Dallas-based logistics software provider Slync.io reportedly failing to pay employees and vendors on time, according to reports by The Athletic June 10 and Business Insider Tuesday. The layoffs bring back memories of the early stage of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020 when well-known early-stage logistics technology providers Flexport and Freightos both announced preemptive layoffs ahead of what they feared would be a lockdown-induced economic downturn. That, of course, never materialized, and in fact freight demand swung back with a vengeance through 2021. The difference this time is it is unclear as to whether a range of macro dynamics — from rising inflation to higher interest rates to the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict — will dampen freight demand. More relevant to the logistics technology market, the broader issue is whether an economic downturn might hinder discretionary spending on technology. It is far too early to tell. It should be noted that a number of companies have landed funding rounds in recent months, even as the broader venture capital world has become more circumspect about which companies to invest in and the valuations attached to those companies that do land funding. On Wednesday, Chain.io announced an $11 million round. In late May, Latin America–focused digital forwarder Nowports landed a $150 million investment, while a week before that, logistics procurement technology provider Keelvar snagged $24 million. In mid-April, trucking optimization software maker Optimal Dynamics pocketed a $33 million round. The timing of these announcements does not always coincide with the actual funding commitments from venture groups, meaning some of that fundraising could have occurred before the market soured in late February. There is also the issue of whether the logistics technology market is somewhat insulated from a huge crash due to early-stage companies selling into organizations that still have physical goods to move. Even if demand is moderating, freight levels remain at historically healthy levels, and the COVID-19 pandemic underscored shortcomings in shipper and forwarder technology infrastructure. Another potential silver lining for companies in the logistics technology space is that the sector has lagged behind others, such as financial technology and health technology, and therefore has less to fall in case a correction does occur. Outside of a cohort of companies that includes Convoy and Stord, most startups are not unicorns, meaning those with valuations of $1 billion or more. One definite impact of the economic malaise in the technology sector is that planned initial public offerings (IPO) for some of the more high-flying logistics technology companies have been put on hold, a range of investors and watchers have told JOC.com. Whereas companies such as project44, which made no secret of its desire to become public, might have ordinarily targeted an IPO in 2022, public market conditions have delayed those plans. title: Carriers’ antitrust immunity may be next target of US shipping reform
content: Given that OSRA passed with strong bipartisan majorities in both the House and Senate, targeting the antitrust immunity of carriers is seen by some as unfinished business whose passage may not be completely out of reach. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. With the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA) signed into law, further legislation could be in the works given the gaping disconnect between the limited impact of the first re-write of US shipping law in nearly a quarter century and the increasingly vocal demands of the Biden administration to bring down shipping costs in an attempt to curb inflation ahead of midterm elections. The next logical step in reforming shipping law — the elimination of ocean carriers’ antitrust immunity — was briefly proposed earlier this year but shot down due to its potential impact on carriers’ ability to operate within alliances. In opposing the idea, the International Longshoremen’s Association (ILA) in March cited the “upheaval it would create in the industry as well as in the global marketplace.” The issue, however, is that OSRA22 focuses narrowly on detention and demurrage charges and ensuring adequate service for exports, and it’s widely agreed that the law will do little, especially in the near term, to curb elevated freight rates that President Joe Biden recently labeled “outrageous.” “We have to change this,” Biden said in a video on June 9. “The political communication, from especially the US government and President Biden, is significantly at odds with the reality of OSRA,” wrote analyst Alan Murphy, CEO of Sea-Intelligence Maritime Analysis, in his weekly Sunday Spotlight newsletter. Given that OSRA passed with strong bipartisan majorities in both the House and Senate, antitrust immunity is seen by some as unfinished business whose passage may not be completely out of reach. This is despite the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) concluding unequivocally in May that competition in container shipping is “vigorous” and that rates rose to all-time highs last year and remain significantly elevated now not because of collusion, but rather “are the product of the market forces of supply and demand.” “There is not anticompetitive behavior in the ocean container shipping industry,” Jim Newsome, president and CEO of the South Carolina Ports Authority, told JOC.com. “The major carriers have been well-scrutinized under European, Asian, and US regulatory regimes over the last 20 years as antitrust immunity for pricing was removed. The market will continue to define the level of rates.” That is precisely why, when overcapacity dominated the market for years pre-COVID, carriers struggled to be profitable. Return on invested capital was just 2.6 percent for container lines between 1995 and 2016, far lower than marine terminals, freight forwarders, railroads, and trucking, according to a Capital IQ and McKinsey analysis. The reverse happened last year. As vessel space tightened under the strain of COVID-driven consumer spending and growing port congestion, shippers of higher-value goods bid up the price of ocean freight, rather than carriers initiating the price increases. If ocean freight pre-COVID represented less than 1 percent of the retail price of $100 high-end sneakers, for example, a shipper would likely not mind having ocean freight be 3 percent, and thus could tolerate significantly higher prices than shippers with lower-value goods, for whom the higher ocean prices were a much greater burden. But voices of reason from the FMC and other industry leaders have not put the debate to rest, although any further shipping legislation would be vocally opposed by carriers, ports, and others — including labor. “There are people looking at anti-trust immunity. There has been discussion about it and whether it needs to be retained,” Jon Gold, vice president for supply chain and customs policy at the National Retail Federation (NRF), told JOC.com June 20. “There has been a lot of discussion about what this means and what the impact would be.” The potential impact of a revocation of ocean carrier antitrust immunity in the US, which dates back to 1916, would be significant. It would focus on the three major alliances — 2M, Ocean, and THE, which control the dominant share of freight in the east-west trades, although that share has declined in the trans-Pacific as upstarts have launched services to take advantage of sky-high rates. Sources differ on whether eliminating antitrust immunity would spell the end of alliances, but many believe the alliances would be forever constrained, if not eliminated. Ocean carrier executives who spoke with JOC.com believe such an outcome would fundamentally change the industry. They believe, for example, that it would precipitate yet another round of consolidation among all but the largest carriers. The reason is carriers require significant scale to be able to offer competitive sailing frequencies, and even then, services would be further concentrated at major ports, a point made by the ILA. “Vessel sharing agreements are an essential vehicle of the industry’s limited antitrust immunity because they allow carriers to provide customers with more frequent service at a lower cost by sharing vessel space,” said the union representing dockworkers handling containers at ports on the US East and Gulf coasts. “Furthermore, without vessel sharing, there would likely be less service at smaller and medium-size ports.” Analyst Lars Jensen agreed, arguing that eliminating alliances would reduce, not stimulate, competition. “The root of the matter is that vessels have grown to a size where the design of a comprehensive network can only be done with multiple carriers collaborating. Not being able to collaborate would lead each individual carrier to have much fewer weekly services,” Jensen told JOC.com. “This in turn would lead to all carriers focusing their services on the largest port-port combinations — and these would indeed see increased competition. However, many port-port combinations would then lose their direct connection and be relegated to transshipment options.” “This, in turn, could lead to a carrier providing such a specific port-pair as a direct service — de facto creating a situation of just a single carrier offering this particular port pair as a direct service as opposed to the current networks where most such port-pairs are served directly by three different alliances,” added Jensen, also an analyst for JOC.com. Thus, he said, “the consequence would likely be less competition on a significant part of the market.” That is why many are saying in one way or another, “be careful what you wish for.” Contact Peter Tirschwell at peter.tirschwell@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @petertirschwell. © 2026 S&P Global. title: New partnership gives FourKites access to FedEx data trove
content: FedEx has invested an undisclosed amount into FourKites as part of the partnership, with has bolstered the Chicago-based visibility provider’s valuation above $1 billion, CEO Mathew Elenjickal told JOC.com. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. FedEx and visibility software provider FourKites are partnering on a new platform that will allow FourKites to tap into FedEx’s internal data to help shippers improve their multimodal and multicarrier transportation planning and predictive visibility. The partnership, which also entails FedEx investing an undisclosed amount into FourKites, gives Chicago-based FourKites exclusive access to hundreds of milestones FedEx collects from its internal network, FourKites CEO Mathew Elenjickal told JOC.com Tuesday. “There is a lot of data their network is generating that’s not being exposed publicly,” he said. “FedEx exposes 10 to 15 milestones, but internally, they’re collecting roughly 300 scans [on each shipment].” FourKites will get access to all those data points to feed into its machine learning model, Elenjickal said. The resulting product, called FourKites X, is a platform aimed at helping shippers in four areas: dynamic planning across modes on a pre-shipment basis, enhanced visibility based on access to more of FedEx’s data, predictive solutions, and what Elenjickal called “end-to-end supply chain optimization.” “If you do planning and visibility and issue resolution better, you have the tools to do things better end-to-end, to incorporate things like sustainability,” he said. For FourKites customers that also use FedEx, FourKites will get detailed access to those customers’ shipment profiles to help them across the four targeted areas. FourKites will also get access to data from FedEx on non-FourKites customers in an anonymized fashion to feed into its models. The partnership links FourKites, which has built a sizable reputation as a real-time and predictive transportation visibility provider catering to shippers, with FedEx Dataworks, a subsidiary of the Memphis-based integrator that launched in 2021 to better use data from its network. “If the last two years have taught us anything, it’s that companies need to work together in order to work smarter and faster,” FedEx Dataworks CEO Sriram Krishnasamy said in a statement Tuesday. “Our collaboration with FourKites creates a data ecosystem that will deliver a new level of predictability and visibility to help businesses build smarter supply chains in today’s unpredictable and complex business environment.” Elenjickal said FourKites X “covers any mode FedEx offers,” adding the majority of FourKites’ customers are existing FedEx customers as well. “Nearly everybody is using FedEx in some fashion, whether its parcel, [less-than-truckload], airfreight, or customs brokerage,” he said. “We’re bringing the [artificial intelligence and machine learning] tools to the table to help them provide better service levels.” Elenjickal said the partnership benefits FedEx by giving their customers a neutral platform. “FedEx customers not just using FedEx,” he said. “To get value from FedEx data, solutions need to be provider-agnostic, and that’s what FourKites brings to the table.” The partnership ups the ante in a red-hot visibility market where FourKites, its chief rival project44, and a horde of other providers have seen demand increase as shippers grapple with supply and demand volatility. Chief among the intended benefits of the FourKites-FedEx partnership is helping retailers and their suppliers “improve planning to address empty shelves and manufacturing slowdowns” and bring chief financial officers ways to improve inventory management, the companies said in the statement. “[FedEx] hasn’t opened their network data to anyone else before,” Elenjickal said. “This [partnership] has been in the works for years, with the idea of creating unique products.” The investment in FourKites also brings a heavy hitter into the company’s existing investor group, which includes the venture arms of Volvo and Qualcomm, as well as warehousing systems provider Zebra Technologies. Elenjickal said FourKites’ valuation has surpassed $1 billion as of May, up from the $750 million valuation at its last funding round in March 2021. title: Revlon scrambles to stabilize its supply in bankruptcy
content: Revlon may be the first of several supply chain bankruptcies to come. That is to say, when the cosmetics giant filed for Chapter 11 protection last week, it cited as causes a host of complications throughout its supply chain, many of them outside its control and all of which followed years of cash burn and heavy indebtedness. Revlon is a supply chain bankruptcy the same way that (heavily-indebted, long-struggling) J. Crew was a pandemic bankruptcy and (heavily indebted, long-struggling) Toys R Us was a “retail apocalypse” bankruptcy. Still, Revlon went into bankruptcy with a major supply problem, which has exacerbated its financial woes and vice versa, and which the company needs to resolve in short order while at the same time trying to reorganize in Chapter 11. Robert Caruso, a managing director with the turnaround firm Alvarez & Marsal who is serving as Revlon’s chief restructuring officer, laid out the many problems in court papers last week. In short, the company has struggled to acquire materials and inventory as well as labor in manufacturing and logistics. At the same time, vendors have been tightening Revlon’s trade credit, worsening its liquidity issues, and retail customers have imposed fines on the cosmetics company as its inventory issues have turned into late product shipments. None of those problems went away when Revlon filed. And now it is racing to smooth relationships with suppliers — and pay them — so it can meet demand and product orders for the pending holiday season. As Caruso told it, Revlon was seeing strong demand for its products by late spring this year — after its sales tanked in the early phases of the pandemic. The rebound for Revlon tracks with rising sales in beauty. Target, for example, has pointed to strong performance in its beauty category as consumers have started going out more in social settings. But as Revlon’s sales increased, so did supply chain disruptions and competition for raw materials. Caruso said Revlon’s vendors began tightening terms at this time, requiring payment on outstanding amounts or cash in advance for new orders instead of offering 30 to 75 day payment terms as in the past, as well as putting credit holds on the company for overdue payments. “If [Revlon] did not comply, they would simply sell their products to one of the many other willing buyers,” Caruso said. It’s a deadly cycle. Tightened credit terms have strained Revlon’s liquidity and put constraints on its supply, which led to delayed shipments and revenue shortfalls, hurting liquidity further and hurting its ability to procure product. Caruso also nodded to global labor shortages for Revlon and suppliers that led to “higher costs and delays in production and transportation” while “global inflation rose at a rate faster than the Company could pass the increased costs through to its customers.” “If the Company cannot demonstrate an ability to deliver sufficient quantities of its products to its customers, that critical shelf space is at significant risk of being lost.” For all the increases in e-commerce, Revlon’s wholesale relationships with traditional retailers — including Walmart, Target, CVS, T.J. Maxx and other massive chains — are critical to the life of the company. Caruso noted that “if the Company cannot demonstrate an ability to deliver sufficient quantities of its products to its customers, that critical shelf space is at significant risk of being lost.” To serve those retail customers and its other channels, Revlon has a tangled suite of brands and some 8,000 SKUs it sells, with a complicated supply chain behind them given that many of those products have 35 to 40 ingredients comprising them. And there’s competition to acquire those ingredients. “[B]ecause many of the Company’s competitors have more cash on hand, they have been able to build more inventory in advance, invest in stocking up on components and raw materials, and pay up front or a premium where needed to secure additional supplies,” Caruso said. Competitors have even been able to outmuscle Revlon for ingredients when the latter had a purchase order with a vendor, Caruso noted. In turn, Revlon’s manufacturing capacity has wilted with supplies. At the time of filing, Revlon facilities in North Carolina, Florida and Mexico had closed or were within weeks of shutting down because of a lack of supply. If the company can’t “rapidly resume” production, it stands to lose at least $87 million in committed holiday sales and $94 million in new product development sales just in Q4, Revlon said in separate court papers. In the short term, the solution is money. Revlon filed with hundreds of millions of dollars lined up from lenders to fund it through bankruptcy, in what’s known as debtor-in-possession financing. The company also filed with a request to pay key vendors — those deemed “critical” as well as foreign vendors and various vendor claimants — $40.4 million in the interim and $79.4 million on a final basis. The bankruptcy judge overseeing Revlon’s case has signed off on the interim payments. All of this is happening as Revlon — roughly 90 years old and today majority-owned by investor Ronald Perelman’s MacAndrews & Forbes — tries to forge its financial and corporate future. While Revlon’s experience is singular in many ways, it also reflects many of the fears in the market around retail. Debt loads overall have increased since the pandemic. In some cases cheap capital has masked operating weakness, looming as a hidden risk in supply chains. Retailers, meanwhile, face rapidly downshifting consumer demand for discretionary goods as the cost of supply, freight, fuel and other inputs continue rising for businesses. As for Revlon, the company has set up a restructuring committee to review any reorganization plans, as well as any sale of some or most or all of the company’s assets. Revlon has signaled that it intends to cut its debt and reorganize in bankruptcy, but it still has to put forward a detailed plan for how to do that. Whatever it hashes out with lenders, the company’s future hinges on the present. If it can’t procure supply to meet retailer demand going into the holidays and next year, the days ahead will be that much darker for the maker of “Super Lustrous” lipsticks.

title: OSRA-22 rules on detention, demurrage go into effect
content: Under the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022, carrier lines now must certify that any detention and demurrage fees are reasonable, or they will be subject to fines. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The part of new US shipping reform that governs detention and demurrage fees went into effect Friday, with container lines now forced to certify that fees are reasonable and incentivize cargo movement. Under the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22), signed into law June 16 by President Joe Biden, carriers are subject to fines if they charge detention and demurrage for situations beyond a shipper’s control, such as the inability to move cargo because of congestion, a lack of appointments, or a shortage of chassis. While detention and demurrage were contentious issues long before the pandemic, complaints have flared in the past two years because of frustration with fees amid historic US port congestion. The Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) said the agency has been struggling to keep up with calls, but has been prioritizing investigations. Hapag-Lloyd was fined an $882,220 US civil penalty over detention charges in April, upped to $2 million in June, while Wan Hai was hit with an $850,000 fine in May to settle a detention case. Peter Friedman, executive director of the Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC), told JOC.com that shippers hoped for immediate action, adding carriers have suggested that OSRA’s provisions not take effect until the lengthy rulemaking process was complete. “Perhaps most importantly, in my view, is the message sent to the carriers and their attorneys: their top priority should now be compliance with the new law, not trying to delay or undermine it via rulemakings,” Friedman said in a statement. As carriers look to navigate the new law, marine terminal operators (MTO) have been removed from the final version of OSRA’s certification and invoicing requirements, and per Congress can continue charging reasonable fees to move cargo. The National Association of Waterfront Employers (NAWE) said MTOs are working with their ocean carrier customers to ensure they are following OSRA’s obligations when invoicing detention and demurrage on an ocean carrier’s behalf. “NAWE’s members are working diligently to create the transparency that Congress sought to create in the billing process, although there will be challenges based on the need to immediately implement new processes and update electronic billing systems, when possible,” the NAWE told JOC.com. Marine terminals haven’t all welcomed the new laws surrounding detention and demurrage because it will dull their ability to levy fees as incentive to move cargo and equipment — pushing back that the fees are not used to generate revenue. SSA Marine President Ed DeNike said the increased regulatory burden will result in more paperwork and further slow operations because marine terminals will be more reluctant to impose storage fees, and the cost of both will ultimately be borne by shippers. While detention and demurrage rules have been in place since May 2020, when the FMC created the interpretive rule on detention and demurrage under the shipping act, the rule has become self-executing law under OSRA. Other provisions of shipping law will take months or even years to sort out. Detention and demurrage provisions apply to any charge assessed or invoice issued by, or on behalf of, a common carrier, and apply to imports and exports regardless of whether the charge is assessed or invoiced electronically or in paper form, the FMC General Counsel said in a statement Friday. title: Resin, packaging constraints create headwinds for medtech: Medtronic
content: Medtronic is seeing signs of a supply chain recovery and is working on its pricing strategy as inflation rises, CEO Geoff Martha said Tuesday at the Goldman Sachs Global Healthcare Conference. Disruptions in the company’s supply chain, particularly for semiconductors and resins, helped lead to a 1% drop in Medtronic’s sales in its fourth quarter, which ended April 29. Martha said as recently as last month that the company expected the supply chain issues to continue in the fiscal first quarter. On Tuesday, Martha said those supply problems may be easing. “We’re seeing the resin issue get better. We’re seeing the packaging issue get better. It’s going to still take some time and we factored that in,” Martha said at the conference. “So, it’s going to affect our Q1 as well [but] we have line of sight to these things abating, especially by the second half of our fiscal year.” Covid-linked disruptions are likely to permanently change supply chains, said Martha. Given the “new environment and geopolitical situation,” he said Medtronic is now building more resiliency into its operations to better “balance efficiency and resiliency,” Adding resiliency will involve “some incremental cost,” Martha said, but he said the changes would generate savings that outweigh that cost. At the root of the problem is the fact that Medtronic’s M&A-driven growth resulted in what Martha called a “pretty fragmented approach” to supply. “Because we’re fragmented, there’s a lot of opportunity for cost savings, just from centralizing,” Martha said. “We decided to centralize our supply chain to really drive some more standards, leverage our scale. The idea there is to get significantly more cost-of-goods-sold productivity over time than we had over the last 20 years,” he said. Martha said he plans to increase R&D spending in part by trimming expenses across the company to free up cash. Medtronic’s R&D spending is below the target it set last year. Martha said he expects 2023 to be “a bit of a transition year” because of inflation. Rising inflation has medtech companies considering how and if they can pass their extra costs on to customers. Medtronic has assembled a centralized pricing team to model the effects of pricing changes and guide new pricing strategies, said Martha. Across the industry, said Martha, medtech firms are reversing the mindset that has them build regular low-single-digit price decreases into forecasts. “Excluding maybe the China [volume-based purchases], we expect to reverse that this year,“ Martha said. “You’re taking a little risk, but I think it’s necessary. We’re spending time on this, putting together a centralized pricing team to help do the modeling and guide us and help us facilitate the strategies.” Martha also used the investor event to provide an update on Medtronic’s robotics program and on the feedback the company has received from real-world use in Europe and demonstrations in the U.S. “We’re bullish on it but I want to make sure of two things. One, if we can incorporate some of these tweaks that we heard from the European surgeons. These aren’t major design changes but some tweaks. And two, I want to make sure from a supply chain perspective, it’s ready to go because it does have a lot of chips. It has a lot of things in it that are in short supply right now. So, we don’t want to launch it and have to pull it back,” Martha said. Martha said he remains confident the robotics project will justify the company’s investment and pointed to the potential to drive growth by going from open to minimally invasive to robotic surgery. “Being a player in robotic surgery, soft tissue robotic surgery, is important for the overall health of your surgery business,” Martha said. “Surgeons want to work with somebody that has the complete portfolio.” China’s move to volume-based purchases is one of several changes in the world’s most populous country that may hurt Medtronic’s surgical innovations unit in the coming years, Martha said. “The market is still going to grow double digits, and it’s going to grow double digits for a long time. But there is more risk coming from some of the pricing and coming from just overall geopolitics,” in the Chinese market, said Martha. “I still am bullish on investing in China, but you do have to consider the risks and that does impact how we make those investments.”

title: Convoy injects brokerage tech into MercuryGate TMS
content: Convoy for Brokers, launched in November, is software designed for other freight intermediaries to drive loads into Convoy’s base of truckload carriers. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Freight broker Convoy is partnering with transportation management system (TMS) provider MercuryGate to integrate the intermediary’s “Convoy for Brokers” product into MercuryGate’s platform. MercuryGate’s TMS is widely used by brokers to manage tendering of loads to carriers, while Convoy for Brokers is designed to give other brokers access to capacity in Convoy’s network of more than 400,000 trucks. The integration adds to an existing multi-year partnership between Convoy and MercuryGate built around application programming interfaces (APIs) that give MercuryGate’s broker customers access to Convoy’s network. The addition of Convoy for Brokers functionality allows brokers to post loads to Convoy’s marketplace, while the technology automates pricing, load matching, compliance checks, and appointment scheduling. The integration is an example of the blurring lines between pure software providers and technology-focused intermediaries, including burgeoning partnerships intended to deliver complementary products. Ordinarily, software vendors would be expected to build or acquire the full range of solutions their customer bases seek. But the Convoy-MercuryGate integration partnership allows the TMS provider to add capacity and automate the process of securing that capacity without having to develop that functionality itself. “We know that for [customers] to grow sustainably, they need access to competitive, real-time rates,” Jeffrey Varon, MercuryGate's chief strategy officer, said in a statement Thursday. For Convoy, the partnership is aimed at further providing a steady stream of loads to its base of carriers, with the aim of keeping them in-network as much as possible. “The only way to achieve [our] mission is by partnering with other technology platforms and freight providers to share the benefits of a digital freight network,” Brooks McMahon, chief business development officer at Convoy, said in the statement. Meanwhile, Convoy has expanded another partnership with forwarder Flexport, which launched in June 2021 to tie together Flexport’s international moves that flow to Convoy’s domestic freight network. Last week, the two companies announced they were enhancing visibility in transload moves, given a rise in demand for those services. “Since our partnership was formed, massive delays at both ocean and rail ports have led to changes in shipping patterns,” Flexport Product Manager Grant Thain wrote in a June 22 blog. “More containers are being transloaded to avoid inland bottlenecks. Much of the transloaded cargo is already delayed due to port backlogs, so companies are eager to understand exactly where their cargo is located.” Transloading occurs when cargo is unloaded from an ocean container and loaded into a domestic 53-foot trailer. The companies said they are now providing GPS visibility on most Flexport loads booked through Convoy. “Surfacing live GPS locations of Convoy loads on the Flexport platform is just the first of many product milestones,” Thain wrote. “For this use case, the technical work required was not terribly complex – much of the infrastructure was in place on both sides. This shows that we don’t have to build highly technical, time-consuming products to add tremendous value to our clients.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. title: New House legislation would entice carriers to haul US exports
content: US farmers have lost an estimated $25 billion in agricultural exports in the past six months because of exporting issues, according to Zippy Duvall, president of the American Farm Bureau. Photo credit: Bill Cassidy/JOC.com. Ocean carriers would receive “preferential berthing” at US ports in exchange for calling multiple ports in the country or agreeing to carry “significant” volumes of exports under legislation introduced Wednesday in the House of Representatives. The American Port Access Privileges Act, designed as a companion to the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 just signed into law, is meant to jump-start US exports, particularly agricultural goods, according to Representatives John Garamendi and Jim Costa, two California Democrats who co-sponsored the bill. “Foreign exporters’ access to the American market and our consumers is a privilege, not a right,” Garamendi said in a statement. “Cargo ships looking to offload foreign-made products and profit off West Coast ports must provide opportunities for American exports in return.” Giving preferential berthing to individual vessels would, on the surface, seem to be a difficult task, considering it would mean government influence on the business operations of marine terminals and involve a new level of coordinating sailing schedules with carriers. Still, it continues the recent trend of Washington attempting to solve the problems that have vexed the US supply chain for the past two years. “This new preferential berthing will reward ocean carriers that serve both importers and American exporters by moving those vessels to the front of the queue for unloading and loading,” the statement said. “It will similarly incentivize ocean carriers to make second-leg voyages to ports like the Port of Oakland, which is critical for California’s agricultural exporters.” US farmers have lost an estimated $25 billion in agricultural exports in the past six months due to issues exporting from the US, Zippy Duvall, president of the American Farm Bureau, said June 16. And ag exports are expected to decline for a second consecutive year in 2022 due to pandemic-related supply chain disruptions in Asia and continued congestion at major US ports and inland rail hubs. California Senators Dianne Feinstein and Alex Padilla previously voiced their support for the nation’s ag industry in May, urging ocean carriers to provide more containers for exports after the state lost $2.1 billion in ag exports in just a five-month period last year. title: Scan Global becomes latest European forwarder to target Asia-based rival
content: Copenhagen-headquartered Scan Global Logistics said Sea-Air Logistics will become part of the Scan group from July 5. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Scan Global Logistics has become the latest European freight forwarder to target an Asia-based logistics company with a deal to acquire Hong Kong-headquartered Sea-Air Logistics. The move was announced Friday, the same day that French forwarder Geodis confirmed the completion of its acquisition of Singapore’s Keppel Logistics from Keppel Telecommunications and Transportation. The deals boost the European firms’ warehousing and airfreight footprint in Asia and follow two major acquisitions last year – Maersk’s purchase of Hong Kong’s LF Logistics and Kuehne + Nagel’s takeover of China-focused forwarder Apex International Corporation. Copenhagen-headquartered Scan Global Logistics said Sea-Air Logistics (SAL) will become part of the Scan group from July 5. The move follows Scan’s acquisition of SAL's longstanding United Kingdom-headquartered partner, Horizon International Cargo, last October. “Combining the experience and capabilities of Scan and SAL will allow for further expansion in several segments such as consumer electronics, technology, pharma and healthcare,” Scan said in a statement. SAL will increase Scan’s market share on the trans-Pacific, Asia-Europe, and intra-Asia trades through nine warehouses and offices in China, Hong Kong, and Singapore, the firms said. No financial details were released, although all SAL’s management and staff are expected to retain their jobs. Meanwhile, Geodis said completion of the acquisition of Keppel Logistics “increases its contract logistics footprint and e-commerce fulfillment services in Asia-Pacific.” The deal will integrate Keppel’s logistics business, including its fast-growing UrbanFox courier and online fulfilment operations in Singapore, Vietnam, and Malaysia with Geodis’ airfreight, ocean, and road transport networks in Asia, Geodis said. Keppel Logistics also operates more than 2 million square feet of warehousing in Singapore, Malaysia, and Australia that “will complement Geodis’ existing high-tech facilities, including its chemical, ambient temperature, and temperature-controlled storage,” Geodis said in a statement Friday. title: WiseTech’s Bolero buy signal of continued eBL progress
content: No electronic bill of lading provider has yet been able to carve out a dominant position, as container lines have partnered with a range of software vendors to build their own products. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Progress on pushing the container shipping industry toward the use of electronic bills of lading (eBLs) in lieu of paper versions has continued with widely used forwarding software provider WiseTech Global making an acquisition in the space. WiseTech’s purchase last week of UK-based Bolero, for an undisclosed amount, rekindles the Sydney-based software provider’s strategy of building through acquisition, this time adding a tool that lets forwarders offer an eBL product to shipper customers. WiseTech made a flurry of bolt-on acquisitions to its core operating system product, CargoWise, throughout 2017 and 2018. title: Grocers eye improvements for e-commerce fulfillment, in-store operations
content: Picking online orders is still causing headaches for grocers on multiple fronts, with customers often groaning about inadequate substitutions or bruised produce, and in-store shoppers jostling with e-commerce workers to select products in the aisles. Major players like Kroger are looking to solve those dilemmas with dedicated fulfillment sites for online orders and automation that takes the burden of order picking off store associates and gig workers. But many other grocers continue to rely on in-store fulfillment for online orders. Sometimes this is by choice — Walmart, for example, is leaning on its existing retail locations’ proximity to customers to help fulfill online orders — and sometimes it’s due to financial constraints that keep them from investing in off-site e-commerce infrastructure. Sources in the industry outlined three key areas grocers can invest in to help make in-store order picking more efficient while also offering a quality experience to both in-store and online customers: store design, technology and training. As an incentive to step up e-commerce fulfillment, some companies, like SpartanNash and Shipt, have positioned their workers as high-touch personal shoppers and promoted their services as a competitive advantage. SpartanNash relies on its own workers to pick and pack orders for its Fast Lane and Groceries To Go services at close to 120 stores across the Midwest. “What we find is that, as our customers get used to the program and used to [SpartanNash’s personal] shoppers who are working, they’re going to say, ‘I specifically want Maria to shop my order. She knows exactly what I’m looking for,’” said Matt Van Gilder, SpartanNash’s director of digital marketing and commerce. E-commerce fulfillment is a “huge” focus for grocers as they consider their store designs and layouts, said Craig St. Clair, associate principal at Cuningham, an architecture, design and planning firm. But the need for e-commerce infrastructure can vary store-to-store depending on customer demand and online order volume. “It’s a very store-centric thing. Every store has its personality in terms of the customer base around it — if they’re even receptive to doing online shopping,” St. Clair said. Grocers are hesitant to invest in dedicated e-commerce facilities as consumer interest has waned following online shopping surges early in the pandemic, St. Clair noted. Overall, grocers that are seeing high online order volumes are looking to improve shopper flow and carve out dedicated spaces for online order fulfillment inside their stores, St. Clair said, along with Gregory Houck, principal and director of new work at the same firm. Both St. Clair and Houck stressed the importance of grocers being flexible with their store design so they can accommodate e-commerce workers now and, eventually, automation, which Houck said forward-looking grocers are planning for in the next 10 to 20 years. In some cases, grocers are moving dry goods and center store to the back-of-house and accentuating fresh foods departments and meal solutions front-of-house, they noted. This can enhance stores’ “fresh” appeal while also pushing aisle shopping, which can get crowded with online and in-store shoppers, to the margins. Mike Demko, senior vice president and global head of AutoStore Retail, said grocers are carving out dedicated picking spaces inside their stores stocked with fast-moving products. For example, Angelo Caputo’s Fresh Markets, a grocer in the Chicago area, uses 5,000 square feet at its flagship store to create a “fast pick area” stocked with products that have the highest online sales volume, Demko said. “If you think about grocery orders, everybody loves bananas, everybody buys milk, so there’s some items that are much faster sellers than others,” he said, noting that grocers can organize products in those dedicated areas based on how fast they sell instead of following in-store merchandising plans, which are made with in-store shoppers in mind. Grocers and e-commerce providers have been turning to technology solutions to address picking problems, from speeding up the process to improving quality around product selection. For example, Instacart announced earlier this year an in-store navigation tool with an interactive map of the grocery store to help locate products more easily as part of its rollout of features and services for shoppers. Last year, Walmart said it saw customer acceptance of substitutions jump more than 95% after pivoting from a manual process for identifying substitutions to employing deep learning artificial intelligence for online grocery orders. Walmart noted deep learning allows it to consider hundreds of factors, like size, type, brand and price, when determining recommendations for out-of-stocks. The effectiveness and usage of technology to drive picking efficiencies can vary depending on how a store operates, how much e-commerce volume it has, how quick the fulfillment window is and whether humans or robots are doing the picking and packing, sources noted. Speed and order volume, in particular, may determine which picking technology solutions retailers turn to. A roughly 40,000-square-foot grocery store that uses software and scanning technology to pick multiple orders at a time from stores shelves can assemble roughly 60 to 90 units an hour. A “fast pick area,” like Caputo’s, more than doubles that, picking about 150 to 180 units per hour, said Demko, who previously headed up pick-and-pack software company Locai Solutions, which AutoStore acquired last year. Demko also formerly oversaw operations at FreshDirect. Automation, like robotic picking technology in the back of a store, can bring those numbers up to 400 units per hour, he said. While some automation upgrades remain out of reach for many stores, mainly due to high cost, sources said they expect robots to eventually take over e-commerce grocery fulfillment. “The killer of productivity in a store environment is travel distance,” said Demko, noting that grocers need to maximize the amount of work done within that distance or minimize how far pickers walk. The higher the e-commerce order volume, the more grocers can benefit from bundling batch picking — shopping more than one order at once — with zone-based picking, where certain pickers only focus on pulling items from different aisles, Demko said. A bagging-and-tagging process where pickers scan barcodes on the products and the bags they belong in can help with that consolidation process downstream, along with ensuring items don’t end up in the wrong bags for different orders, he added. “The benefits of that batch-zone pick process are really about throughput and volume. If I’m only doing a few orders an hour, the amount of orders that might have items in common gets lower and lower,” Demko said. While efficient, batch picking isn’t always the speediest option and can potentially slow down rapid delivery service for one-hour or faster orders, he said. Demko said it’s important that the mobile application used by the pickers is easy to use and aligns with visual cues in the cart, like knowing which customer’s bags are where. The software must work for all of the areas where picking takes place, from the sales floor to the backroom to designated “fast pick” areas. Grocers can leverage data from picking solutions to measure and analyze factors like productivity levels and order accuracy and then look for ways to become even more efficient, he said. While technology may speed up the picking process, working fast can run the risk of making quality-control mistakes. That’s where training comes in: “At the end of the day, technology is only as good as the people who use it,” Demko said. Quality control, which is included in worker training, can play a big role in customer satisfaction and cut down on order returns, sources noted. While technology and store design can help people find the pick the correct brand of avocado quickly, the picker ultimately decides which products meet the customer’s expectation for ripeness and quality. When Demko ran operations at FreshDirect, he said the training mindset there was: “Imagine you’re picking for your grandmother.” “You’ve got to get that quality mindset, which is: When you pick up that leaf of that head of lettuce, look at it and make sure there isn’t a leaf wilting on it … make sure you’re opening up the eggs and make sure there’s nothing broken,” he said. Consumers have been especially reluctant to trust workers to pick fresh produce, meat and other perishables for them, making trust and quality control important to the picking process. Store employees who pick online orders can also help manage shrink by setting aside products they identify as spoiled or not high quality, Demko said. Shipt, which promotes the high-touch service provided by its personal shoppers as a key differentiator in the e-commerce delivery race, provides an “education produce guide” for its Shipt Shopper community. The guide covers three main areas: sight, smell and storage, according to a post from the company in late March. For example, Shipt encourages its shoppers to look for signs of dehydration, like wrinkling and shriveling, to help gauge freshness and to squeeze items like grapes and melons to determine the firmness. “[A] great tip for picking out grapes is taking a look at the vine. Green vines mean the grape was freshly picked and handled properly in transport,” Shipt said in the blog. SpartanNash workers receive training in a variety of areas for order picking, like bagging 101, how to understand expiration dates, and how to determine the quality and ripeness of produce. The training, which was developed in-house and is required for all of the company’s personal shoppers, also delves into skills like identifying produce and the right types of meat. SpartanNash puts a “huge” emphasis on training to make its employees the “eyes and ears of the customer” and ensure customer satisfaction, Van Gilder said. Both Shipt and SpartanNash are leaning heavily into worker training, aiming to have top-notch service fuel attachments between customers and specific pickers and help lock in customer loyalty. “We’re training our personal shoppers to be pickier than the customers who shop themselves,” Van Gilder said. Correction: A previous version of this story misstated Gregory Houck’s role at Cuningham. He is principal and director of new work. Clarification: This story was updated with additional information about SpartanNash’s delivery coverage.

title: AscendTMS, electronic insurance partner aim to aid small fleets
content: AscendTMS, which has carrier, broker, and shipper customers, has long viewed partnerships with adjacent software vendors as a way to expand the value it provides to users, according to CEO Tim Higham. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Transportation management system (TMS) provider AscendTMS is partnering with online fleet insurance supplier CarrierHQ to target small truckload fleets that struggle with the process of acquiring coverage. Florida-based AscendTMS has thousands of carrier, broker, and shipper users who are attracted by the product’s low cost and fast implementation schedule, as well as access to ancillary tools available through integrations. The partnership will allow small fleets that use AscendTMS for dispatch management, accounting, and driver and load connectivity to get native access to instant insurance quotes. “An overwhelming request we get again and again from our fleet users is the ability to quickly quote and bind competitively priced liability, physical damage, and cargo insurance coverage,” AscendTMS CEO Tim Higham said in a statement Wednesday. “They want the ability to quote and bind quickly, while also getting credit for safe driving.” Small Fleet Advantage, CarrierHQ’s product, uses coverage from global insurance provider Aon and allows carriers to get online quotes, buy coverage, and make monthly adjustments based on driving data from electronic logging devices (ELDs). Drivers can reduce their insurance costs as much as 30 percent based on their driving record, CarrierHQ said in the statement. The Small Fleet Advantage integration is just the latest for partner-friendly AscendTMS, which connects to a range of load boards, load matching engines, invoice factoring and carrier payment portals, and major transportation visibility and ELD providers. CarrierHQ is its first insurance partner. The importance of putting easy-to-use, online-based insurance products in the hands of small operators has become clearer in recent years. London-based Loadsure in March landed a funding round to help build its instant insurance products for carriers, shippers, and brokers. “Carriers can get truck liability, physical damage, and cargo coverage within our software,” Higham told JOC.com Wednesday. “This is a big deal for the market, as insurance is one of the largest costs to carriers, behind only fuel and labor, and its cost has been rising fast for the past few years.” More broadly, the partnership with CarrierHQ can be seen as part of the growing array of tools available to independent owner-operators and small carriers, a promising sign for shippers that rely on the capacity smaller operators provide. The solutions, which range from TMSs to back-office tools to optimization and finance products, are primarily designed to make small carriers more efficient and to keep them solvent in down cycles. But they also allow small operator capacity to be directly visible to shippers and brokers, whereas capacity buyers have previously only discovered small operators through transactional load board interactions. title: Hong Kong extends vessel-sharing exemption for carriers, but cuts validity period
content: Hong Kong competition regulators have trimmed a year from the extension they granted for the block exemption for ocean carriers’ vessel-sharing agreements. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Competition watchdogs in Hong Kong have followed those in Singapore and extended the block exemption for ocean carriers’ vessel-sharing agreements, and, similar to Singapore, have cut the validity period, citing the current turmoil in the market. The Hong Kong Competition Commission (HKCC) said Thursday while the original anti-trust exemption in 2017 was to last five years, “it is only being renewed for a further four years” to August 8, 2026. “This is in light of the continuing impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the prevailing market conditions which warrants a review within a shorter time frame,” the commission said in a statement. Similar reasons were given by Competition and Consumer Association of Singapore to cut the validity period of the block exemption to three years from five years. “A duration of three years will provide sufficient legal certainty and lead time for investments, while also allowing CCCS to conduct more regular reviews to ensure that the block exemption remains relevant and current to conditions within the industry,” the association said in a statement. Singapore’s exemption applies to vessel-sharing and feeder service price discussion agreements. The action by both jurisdictions comes as the European Commission (EC) is also facing increasing pressure to review container shipping’s exemption from competition law after the US launched regulatory probes into the sector. By comparison, China has made the Shanghai Shipping Exchange responsible for policing carrier conduct, which includes the requirement for rate filing and discussing changes with shippers, while also calling carriers to meetings if authorities feel lines are abusing their position. text: Hong Kong extends vessel-sharing exemption for carriers, but cuts validity period [SEP] Hong Kong competition regulators have trimmed a year from the extension they granted for the block exemption for ocean carriers’ vessel-sharing agreements. title: Supply chain disruption changed buying patterns in 2022's first half
content: Businesses have gone above and beyond to secure supply in the first half of 2022. After transportation delays, worker constraints and global uncertainty led to supplier slowdowns, many companies had to rethink their buying patterns. Some expanded their sourcing pool, while others inked long-term agreements with vendors to jointly add capacity. One business even sent its own workers to a supplier factory to speed up deliveries. We’ve rounded up some of our most popular procurement stories of H1. Take a look to see how businesses have worked to lessen the impact of higher costs, longer lead times and a lack of raw materials.

title: Trade groups demand EU review carrier anti-trust exemption
content: Trade groups complain that the benefits of the block exemption enjoyed by shipping lines in Europe are not being shared with the rest of the economy. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Ten trade organizations dependent on container shipping have demanded the European Commission immediately launch a review of carriers’ exemption from competition law to allow time for changes to be made before the block exemption expires in April 2024. The demand for an urgent review of Europe’s Consortia Block Exemption Regulation turns up the heat on the European Commission following a report earlier this month by the International Transport Forum (ITF) that called for greater government regulation of container shipping to ensure fair competition. The trade organizations representing shippers, forwarders, ports, terminals, and intermodal service providers said in a joint statement Monday that the benefits of the block exemption enjoyed by shipping lines are not being shared with the rest of the economy, which is “in itself a compelling reason” to begin an urgent review. “The effects of lockdowns on the production of goods and the shifts in demand due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic were certainly significant,” the groups said. “But the ability of the shipping industry to collectively manage these impacts and at the same time generate profits totaling over $186 billion in 2021, at the expense of the rest of the supply chain and ultimately Europe’s consumers, demonstrates that something is wrong.” Signatories to the joint statement cover a wide range of carrier customers, including the Global Shippers’ Forum, European Shippers’ Council, the European Association for Forwarding, Transport, Logistics and Customs Services (CLECAT), and the International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations (FIATA). The block exemption outlines the conditions under which liner shipping alliances can provide joint services without violating EU antitrust rules. But the statement said the regulation allowed carriers to avoid “many of the checks and balances of EU competition law” and exchange commercially sensitive information to manage the number and size of ships deployed, and the frequency of sailings. “European businesses and other parties in the supply chain have suffered huge disruption to the movement of goods by container shipping since the regulation was last renewed in April 2020, with many sailings being cancelled or diverted to other ports, and ports being bypassed at short notice,” the statement noted. “At the same time shipping rates have more than quadrupled on many routes and continue to remain three to four times higher than in 2019 before the pandemic.” Short-term rates from Asia to North Europe valid for 88 days or less are currently at $5,753/TEU, almost seven times higher than during the same week in pre-pandemic 2019, according to rate benchmarking platform Xeneta. Long-term contract rates on Asia–North Europe of $5,151/TEU are almost six times that of the same week in 2019. On the Asia–US West Coast trade, the current short-term rate of $6,683/FEU and the long-term rate of $7,337/FEU are both six times higher than the rates recorded in the same week in 2019. In their letter to the European Commission (EC), the signatories highlighted the investigations conducted in the US by the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), which resulted in President Joe Biden in June signing into law the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22), “addressing many of the grievances of users and services suppliers to the container shipping lines.” It was the first major US shipping reform in more than two decades, giving maritime regulators greater oversight over container storage fees and the ability to monitor whether ocean carriers are adhering to revised rules on loading exports. But not all the US probes found in favor of shippers. An FMC fact-finding study (FF29) released in May concluded unequivocally that competition in container shipping was “vigorous” and that rates did not rise to all-time highs last year and remain significantly elevated not because of collusion, but rather “are the product of the market forces of supply and demand.” This was a point highlighted by John Butler, president and CEO of the World Shipping Council, who told JOC.com earlier this month that liner shipping is “a very closely monitored industry” and that carriers actively compete in the global marketplace. While the European Commission has not yet launched a formal evaluation, EC spokesperson Maria Tsoni told JOC.com recently that a “fact finding exercise” has begun to collect information from carriers operating on European trades, which will feed into a review of the block exemption regulation that expires on April 25, 2024. “Before it expires, the commission will evaluate its impact and relevance in order to determine whether it should be prolonged and, if so, under which conditions,” she said. However, the shipper and forwarder groups say a formal review is urgently needed as it will require all parties to submit evidence and arguments on how the container shipping market can operate in a way that is “fair and transparent to all parties in the maritime supply chain.” “This should include consideration of new measures and mechanisms and should allow sufficient time for these to be considered and implemented before the expiry of the current regulation in April 2024,” the joint statement said.
